Oṃ, salutation to Paramaśiva, whose body is the nectar of one's own self.
Now begins the *Stavacintāmaṇi*,
composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa.
Accompanied by the commentary composed by Śrī Kṣemarāja: When the sun of ultimate reality shines forth,
the entire darkness of ignorance perishes.
At that time, even the wise, though possessing stainless vision, do not perceive the manifold expansion of worldly existence. || 1 ||
Salutations eternally to Śiva, the performer of the five cosmic acts,
who illuminates the ultimate reality of one's own self as consciousness and bliss.
By means of the streams of consciousness flowing everywhere, which are rich with the bliss of internal vibration and movement and which intensely overflow with external vibration,
[the world is pervaded].
Sprinkling the universe, he bows to his own self, Śambhu. || 3 ||
(2) This which has surged forth with the force of the crushing impact of the mountain of discernment from the ocean of Nārāyaṇa’s own heart—
The wise among you, O learned ones, should extract this elixir of praise for Śrī Śaṅkara and savor it here. || 4 ||

Here, at the beginning of the hymn, the author of the hymn speaks in order to contemplate, during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), the immersion into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord— which is one’s own self— as revealed through the true tradition (*satsaṃpradāya*) shown in all the Upaniṣads.
Victorious is she who, gazing with sweet speech that captivates the heart, brings forth exalted bliss—
The Greatness is the Supreme Lord. || 1 ||

The Supreme Lord, whose nature is light and bliss, whose form is embraced by Parāvāk— the very essence of the power of sovereignty consisting of supreme bliss— by means of this very power [manifests as] Śiva, Mantramaheśvara, and Mantreśvara.
The speech *paśyantī* consists of the subjects (*pramātṛ*) of the pure paths (*adhvan*), whose nature is the unmanifested self (*vijñānākala*) through the power of mantra;

the speech *madhyamā* consists of the manifestation of the lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*) such as Maṇḍalī, Śrīkaṇṭha, Krodheśa, Vīrabhadra, the hundred Rudras, Ananta, and Bhuvaneśvara; and [the speech *vaikharī*] consists of the lords of the worlds beyond these.

(Page 3) [The power of speech] which culminates in the various *pralayākalas* and *sakalas*, which manifests as the manifold expansion of those respective diverse forms, and which is pervaded by each preceding power of speech.

Illuminating the *vaikharī* speech within its own substrate, [the Supreme Lord] fashions the manifold variety of the universe through the process of descent (*avaroha*). Thus, even at the level of the *sakala* subject, which is dominated by *vaikharī*, there is indeed no separation from the triad of speech known as *parā*, *parāparā*, and *madhyamā*, according to the aforementioned pervasion. For this very reason:
Desiring to bestow grace, the Blessed One, preceded by the pacification of the *vaikharī* and *madhyamā* stages,
emerged into the state of *paśyantī*; having manifested that [consciousness]— which extends up to the aforementioned *anāśrita-śiva*—
as the object of knowledge (*vedyatvena*), he caused [the disciple] to enter into it by ascending through the stages of the existence of the self as both the known and the knower.
The meaning of the sentence here is: "He who possesses devotion exists with supreme excellence.
As for the meaning of the individual words: the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the conscious self (*cidātman*), is victorious;
He exists with excellence over the entire universe, from Himself down to the earth. Of what kind? [He is superior] in comparison to *vaikharī* and *madhyamā* speech.

This is the excellent Paśyantī, which has explained the ultimate reality (paramārtha), whose nature is an uninterrupted, continuous manifestation without sequential division, and which pervades speech such as Madhyamā and others; by her being perceived— vividly pulsing with a form that has emerged clearly— therefore...

(On page 4: Thus, the mind (*citta*), which consists of the intermediate state (*madhyamā*) and produces sequential conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations mounted upon the intellect (*buddhi*), as well as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which, through association with that [mind], serves as the substratum for *vaikharī* speech— the manifestation of phonemes— [are both included].

By her who carries away— that is, completely pacifies— by her very nature; and by her who is being perceived— in a form that reaches to the limit of the non-supported— through the pacification of the state of being a knower, appearing as the very essence of the object of knowledge,
she has become the cause by which [the soul] is uplifted— that is, led to the path of recognition.

He is the self of supreme speech (*parāvāk*), whose majesty is bliss; by him, having first stilled all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and emerged from the plane of *paśyantī*, he causes even the state of the *anāśrita* (the Unsupported) to appear as an object of knowledge once it has ascended through those [successive] streams, thereby unfolding the state of the supreme subject who is the supreme non-duality consisting of ultimate bliss.

The meaning is that the Supreme Lord bestows grace. And this very means of immersion (*samāveśopāya*) is taught as the essence among all secret doctrines. As it is said in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*: "For one who thinks of nothing at all, through the awakening by the Guru..."
That possession which arises is declared to be Śāmbhava.
Thus [it is said]. Our supreme teacher, the venerable author of the *Pratyabhijñā*, also stated:
"Through the abandonment of conceptual construction and through one-pointedness, one gradually attains the state of Lordship.
(Page 5)
Thus it is said; and in the *Śrījñānagarbha* as well:
"O Mother, having abandoned all mental activities, [one attains] that which is radiant, being free from the dependence on the pursuit of the functions of the senses in every respect."
But by remaining steadfast through your power, men immediately experience that supreme state which flows with the nectar of untiring and unequaled bliss.
Thus: for example, by a certain heart-captivating young woman, who gazes longingly with sweet speech that delights her beloved, and who is herself being looked upon due to their mutual passion—
the greatness of her bliss is inferred from the manifestation of all the *sāttvika* emotions, such as the rising of horripilation (*romāñca*).

"May a certain Lord be victorious"; likewise, by the power of resonance (*anuraṇana-śakti*), there is a paronomastic suggestion (*śleṣadhvani*) that this [Lord] as well is one's own Self, whose essence is Paramaśiva, according to the sequence of explanation [already given]. The nature of Paśyantī and the other levels of speech has been stated by the venerable Bhartṛhari as follows:
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all succession withdrawn;
she is the light of her own nature within, the subtle, imperishable Speech.
Taking up the intellect as its substrate and following the form of sequential succession,
the intermediate speech (madhyamā vāk) proceeds by transcending the activity of the vital breath.

When the wind is released through the various locations [of articulation], speech in its manifest form (vaikharī)— which assumes the apprehension of phonemes— is dependent upon the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa) for those who employ it.
(6) Thus [ends the first section]. || 1 ||
Having thus praised the Śāmbhavī ground, in which power is predominant,
he speaks in order to praise that in which the Power (Śakti) is predominant: "He who is expansive, [possessing] the awakening of glorious compassion..."
Possessing the perfection of supreme bliss and having his majesty illuminated by wisdom,
that unconquered one is victorious. || 2 ||

He—the Blessed One; the Unconquered—surpassing all, is victorious. Grasping Him alone as the supreme excellence, we enter into Him. Śrī is the supreme splendor of consciousness, the foundation for the manifestation of the power of all causes. Dayā is the supreme power of will (*icchā-śakti*), whose nature is the grace toward the universe. Bodha is...

The power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), supreme bliss (*paramānanda*)—which is the power of sovereignty (*svātantryaśakti*)—prosperity (*saṃpat*), which consists of the abundance of the form of one's own manifestation, is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). "Śrī, compassion, awakening, supreme bliss, and prosperity"—that is *śrī-dayā-bodha-paramānanda-saṃpat*; by that.
He who is expanded— that is, completely full— by means of the fivefold power whose nature is the expansion of consciousness, will, knowledge, bliss, and action; for that very reason...

Because it is inclined toward the universal grace, by means of *vidyā*— that is, through the power of pure *vidyā* whose nature is the manifestation of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "I" and "this," in the form of the realization "I alone am everything"—
it is "highly illumined," meaning it has been made manifest to those to be graced as consisting of the supreme non-duality.
Māhātmya—by which there is the expansion of knowledge and action. || 2 ||

Having thus praised the form of the Lord in which power (śakti) is predominant, he speaks in order to praise that in which the individual soul (nara) is predominant: "To him in whom the bindu and nāda are expanding..."
Salutations to the one whose self consists of pure nectar, to the ocean of milk that is Śaṅkara, who possesses infinite light. || 3 ||

Śam: He who effects the highest good (*śreyas*), which consists of the manifestation of supreme non-duality (*parādvaya*), is like the ocean of milk because he possesses qualities such as transparency, density of light, delightfulness, and being the locus of all perfections; to him be *namaḥ*—that very reality, through the method of bowing down with one’s body and so forth.
(Page 8) We enter [into Him]. Into what kind of Śaṅkara-ocean of milk?—
[Into that] "possessing an expanding *bindu* and *nāda*," where *bindu* and *nāda* are constantly and eternally expanding through [the stages of] Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and so forth.

He is one whose *bindu* and *nāda*— which are the powers of knowledge and action consisting of essential identity (*sāmarasya*)— emanate through the form of the universal self (*viśvātman*), who has entered into the manifestation of supreme non-duality (*parādvaita*) up to the limit of the knowable (*vedya*).
For such is the Supreme Lord, whose nature is light (*prakāśa*).

Consisting of the powers of knowledge and action abiding in a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), which is another synonym for the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), and while manifesting upon its own ground, it first brings forth the state of Anāśrita Śiva, which consists in the concealment of one's own self;
then [it brings forth] Sadāśiva, in whom the power of knowledge is predominant, and Īśvara, in whom the power of action is predominant.

Having manifested Śuddhavidyā, which is the nature of the cause of that [Māyā], and Māyā, which consists of the manifestation of contraction; and subsequently having shown Vidyā and Kalā, whose essence is the powers of contracted knowledge and action;
[he manifests] the plane of prāṇa and apāna, which is denoted by the terms bindu, nāda, and śabda, and whose nature is the intensification of that contraction.
Having delineated that which serves as the substratum for the entire series of instruments (the senses),
and having further manifested the plane of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) characterized by the varying degrees of contraction of knowledge and action,
[he manifests] the sense-faculties of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), which consist of the power of knowledge and possess contractions attained through successive gradations.
They are manifested in forms ranging up to the appearance of awakening;
likewise, the organs of action consist of the power of action characterized by extreme contraction, and in that very same way.
Expanding [the consciousness] up to the appearance of objects such as the syllables to be uttered and those to be grasped,

and having caused the light of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) to enter by bringing all objects— beginning with the task of awakening— to a state of identity with the light of the external senses, [he does so] by means of touching the stages of Vidyā and Kalā.

Having entered the state of Sadāśiveśa, manifesting Himself solely through His own power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), He remains eternally engaged in the playful swing of such descent and ascent;

therein, the principles of necessity (*niyati*), time (*kāla*), and attachment (*rāga*) are projected by means of knowledge (*vidyā*) and limited agency (*kalā*) alone, along with the vital breaths of inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*).

The principle of the male (puṃstattva) has been described as that which, having entered within the principles of Vidyā and Kalā, impels Pradhāna through a certain portion [of its power] by means of the objects—the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the gross elements (bhūta). In this way, this Lord [Śiva] possesses the expanding Bindu and Nāda; and for that very reason, because the universe consists of knowledge and action, [He is the source of all].

Even though the Supreme Lord has assumed the manifold variety of the universe, his essence remains pure nectar and the very core of the rasa of supreme bliss; for this very reason, he is infinite— his light is undivided by space, time, or form, because even those [limitations] are of the nature of his own light, otherwise...
Because [the world] is non-existent; and thus, even while expanding in this manner through forms culminating in the human realm,
the ocean of Śiva’s nectar remains entirely full— to that, I offer salutation.

The milk ocean also possesses shimmering droplets, is endowed with the sound of its waves, is pure—meaning brilliantly white—and consists of nectar, while the serpent king shines forth; thus, this is a metaphor based on double entendre (*śleṣopamā*).
The grandfather of the author of the hymn is named Parameśvara, his father is Aparājita, and [his mother] is named Śrīdayā.

His mother was [named] Mātā, and his eldest brother was named Śaṅkara; therefore, experts in traditional narratives maintain that this hymn is also a praise of them, who partake in non-difference from the Supreme Lord. || 3 ||
Thus, having contemplated the Supreme Lord— who is non-dual and the sole ultimate reality— as non-distinct from the stages of Man, Śakti, and Śiva that constitute the universal self,
he extends this very realization of his own self throughout all states until the conclusion of the hymn by means of various [expressions].
O Lord of Ambikā, we hate you with our hymns, yet we praise you and address our prayers to you.
Out of great affection, you have rightly sustained us in all directions. || 4 ||

"O Lord of Ambikā! O Father of the universe, by virtue of being the Father, you have indeed— through the vision of supreme non-duality— held us, 'us' meaning ourselves, 'viśvak' meaning everywhere and at all times in every condition, 'sādhu' meaning perfectly."
He showed favor; how so? Through extreme affection—since you are exceedingly dear to us, and we are always solely devoted to you alone, for that very reason we are also exceedingly dear to you.
As it is said in the Gītā:
"For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me.

Since our hearts are thus united as one, we— out of extreme affection and for the sake of protecting the worldly order while situated in the midst of the world within the sphere of social conduct— do whatever is necessary.
We hate the secret practices and the like with a "closing of the eyes" (gajanimīlanikayā); yet, it is You alone whom we hate.

Indeed, nothing whatsoever appears to us that is not composed of You; thus, even on the plane of the hated and the hater, we are composed of You alone, and never does the impurity of defects such as hatred arise within us.
As he will say:
"O Lord, what fault is there even in a fault? For one who has set out to reach you, what fault can there be?
(page 12)

Thus, even when we, situated in the midst of the world, likewise praise the Vedic rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* and the like, we praise those very things as not being distinct from You; and even when we perform the invocation of deities such as Indra at sacrifices and other rites, we invoke them for Your sake— that is, for You alone.
"We offer the universe as an oblation to the deity that is one's own self, which consists of Śiva. As the Śruti says:
"By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed with the sacrifice...
For this very reason, because there is no fruit distinct from this [offering], there is no...

The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) has not been employed here because there is no intention to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. Furthermore, even though we are situated among those who possess devotion to Your world-transcending state, the fact that we despise Vedic conduct and the like while praising secret conduct and the like is also considered by us to be nothing but You. And thus:
Regarding the two states—the mundane and the supramundane—we consider that which we hate to be You alone;
yet in reality, we praise You, for Your praise consists precisely in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) of the non-dual manifestation of the non-dual.
And thus, in these various conditions such as hatred and praise, [we actually praise] You in reality.
Praising you, we recite the mantra— [we worship] you,
the deity of the mantra, by means of the Great Mantra whose nature is the non-dual awareness of all things.
We speak thus: because of such extreme affection, you have properly and correctly favored us; the meaning is that by your very grace, such great majesty has been manifested for us. || 4 ||
And then, for the sake of withdrawing the union of touch and for the birth of the complete nectar, [he]...
Salutations to Śambhu, the all-pervading Lord, whose essential nature is space and illusion.

Salutation to Him who is the source of well-being (*śambhu*)—that is, *śambhu* because well-being (*śam*) arises from Him—to that All-pervasive One (*vibhava*), the Self of Consciousness (*cidātman*). Of what nature is He? He by whom the connection (*yoga*)—the relationship based on the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within—is withdrawn or destroyed by contact with sense objects (*sparśa*, i.e., sensory domains); and for that very reason, He is the infinite space (*viyat*).

To Him, because His own nature is *māyā* which consists of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) that is perishing; and therefore, for the sake of the birth—that is, the manifestation—of that nectar which is complete, consisting of the expansion of supreme non-duality (*parādvaya*). And thus, the destruction of the bonds—

(Page 14) By bestowing the gift of His own nature, which is full of bliss, the Blessed One, the Great Lord, remains as He Himself while bestowing grace upon those to be graced; thus, it is solely through the method of burning the seed of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Thus it is taught by way of this method: "The devotee, preceded by the pacification of non-apprehension (akhyāti), should enter into the supreme reality.
And it has been said:
"One should uplift oneself by means of the self..."

Thus: the sky—ākāśa—is intangible, the abode of the full moon, of a void-like nature like illusion (māyā), and all-pervasive; thus there is a paronomastic resonance (śleṣadhvani) through the power of reverberation (anuraṇana-śakti), and so it is in what follows as well. || 5 ||
Moreover,
that which is not divided even when things are divided, and which remains undivided even when things are cut asunder;
We bow to that supreme form of the Lord, which is common to all.

We bow to that supreme form of the Lord; through the means of reflecting upon this hymn, we enter into identity with the circle of beings who are to be graced. It is for this very reason that the plural number is used here, as well as previously and subsequently.
(Page 15) It should be applied.

What is that? He says: "Even among those things that are divided"—that is, even while they manifest with distinction as the various *tattvas*, the subjects who preside over them, and the worlds and entities that serve as their substrates—there is that which is not divided.

It is of a single form; likewise, even when those very [forms] are severed—that is, even when they have perished in states such as dissolution—it remains unperished. And for this reason, it is the universal of all (*sarvasāmānya*); its nature is that of the Great Consciousness consisting of perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*), and by the term "universal of all," its distinction from the higher and lower universals (*parāpara-sāmānya*) accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas is indicated.
It has been shown. || 6 ||
Thus,
even greater than the Praṇava’s upper half-mora is the Great Praṇava.
Salutations to Sthāṇu, who is beyond even the cosmic egg and whose nature is devoid of qualities. || 7 ||
Salutation to Sthāṇu—the Blessed One whose form is eternally abiding; of what nature is he?
He is characterized by the upper half-measure of the *praṇava*, which is the extremely subtle part (*mātrā*) consisting of the *samanā* state.
To Him who is even more subtle than that— meaning, whose form is singularly perceptible because His body is imperceptibly minute—
and likewise, who is characterized by Brahmā, the presiding deity over the *Brahmabila* situated within the principle of Power (*śaktitattva*).

The "egg" (*aṇḍa*) extends as far as the Egg of Power (*śaktyaṇḍa*); even beyond that, [it belongs] to the Great One (*mahate*), whose form is unlimited—meaning, to that which pervades it and is itself immeasurable. Likewise, "freedom from qualities" (*nairguṇya*) means that the very absence of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest is itself a "quality"—a property whose nature is the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). And thus:
By means of the sequential utterance of the *praṇava*, and by transcending the stages up to *samanā*,

we enter into the nature of the Lord— which is of one essence with the supreme reality of *unmanā* and which, having pervaded the entire universe up to *samanā*, is pure consciousness alone throughout all states of existence. Thus.
The summary of the meaning. || 7 ||
And then [he beheld] the womb of the cosmic egg, belonging to Him who pervades the sky and whose movement is everywhere.
We praise the power of the Supreme Lord Haṃsa, who is like a female swan. || 8 ||
"Śiva is Haṃsa by virtue of Dharma"—
according to the principle established in the *Svacchanda-tantra* (page 17).
The Supreme Lord alone, whose nature consists of the creation and destruction of the universe and who possesses the attributes of withdrawal and assumption, is the *haṃsa*;
and we praise his power of that very same kind—the *haṃsī* known as *unmanā*.
Preceded by immersion in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that [power], we enter into the essential nature of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). Of what sort is she?
She whose womb contains the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—whose nature has been explained—situated within it with its internal divisions.

Of what kind is the Supreme Lord Swan? He who pervades the void (*vyomavyāpin*), that is, he whose true essence is the Great King of Mantras, and who pervades the void, the state of the Void beyond the void (*śūnyātiśūnyapada*).

Likewise, "all-pervading" (sarvagati) means that whose movement—attainment—is from everywhere, and whose movement—expansive form and luminosity—is everywhere. And there is a simile: for the *haṃsa* (goose), which moves everywhere by gliding through the sky, the female goose (*haṃsī*) carrying an egg within her is its constant companion. || 8 ||
Then, in order to praise the form of Maheśvara, which consists of the absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) that accomplishes even the most difficult tasks, he says:
"Without any collection of material causes..."
They manifest the variegated world upon their own body alone; salutations to that wielder of the trident, who is praiseworthy for his artistic skill.

Salutation to the wielder of the trident, who shines forth through the triad of will, knowledge, and action, which are manifested upon the foundation of the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*). "The world" (*jagat*) is that which undergoes the diversity of various states, beginning from Anāśritaśiva down to the earth (*kṣiti*).

"Citra" means manifold in form; yet that very same "citra," though consisting of the various successive appearances of the Rudras, Kṣetrajñas, and so forth—like a painting—is in reality nothing but the wall itself.
And although it is thus, it appears as if distinct from it, which is wondrous. Thus, the word "citra" is used both distributively and collectively.
"On the wall-less"—on the wall of the Great Void, which consists of the appearance of negation; "they extend"—meaning they have carved it out.
According to the rule that *a*, *mā*, *na*, and *nā* denote negation, the letter *a* signifies negation;
thus, a wall (*bhitti*) that is formless and of the nature of the void is "wall-less" (*abhitti*). How do they extend it?

"Devoid of the accumulation of grasping (*nirupādāna-saṃbhāram*)," where "grasping" (*upādāna*) refers to *māyā*, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and so forth, and "accumulation" (*saṃbhāra*) refers to the collection of auxiliary factors such as karma; having rendered [the world] free from these, because even that which appears as grasping and its auxiliaries is itself a manifestation [of consciousness], it enters right into the midst of the world.
Otherwise, being equivalent to a hare's horn, he would be nothing; thus, the Supreme Lord is to be praised solely for his skill in *kalā*—his own creative power. And this is truly marvelous:
that he brings forth the manifold world (*prapañca*) without any material cause (*upādāna*) or other such factors.
(19) "A painting without a wall"— this is not impossible, for we observe that in the case of mental constructions, dreams, and emanations,
it is the Blessed Consciousness itself that causes the manifestation of those various appearances. 9.

Thus, considering that just as the emergence of the world proceeds from the unobstructed sovereignty of the Blessed One alone, so too is the cessation of saṃsāra appropriately possible from him alone, he prays to the Supreme Lord himself to obtain the knowledge that causes the concealment of māyā.
The milk of the knowledge of Śiva, having been properly extracted from the belly of the water of illusion and purified, flows forth by itself.
Come, come, O swan of Hara, to us! || 10 ||

O Hara-haṃsa, whose true nature has been explained! Come—be present before us; emerge by transcending the stages of the body and so forth. And therefore, even in the state of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*), grant us this knowledge, which consists of the highest good: that "this entire universe is indeed Śiva."
Take root in your mind: "Whatever the Veda declares,
may my mind be intent upon auspicious resolve."

Thus [it is asked]: of what nature is it? It is that which pertains to Māyā, whose form is non-apprehension (akhyāti), and which—by virtue of being fashioned by the limited powers (kalās)—is insentient, consisting essentially of the perception of duality; its "belly" (udara) is the center.
Having properly opened that up through the method of purifying the limited sense of ego (mitāhaṃbhāva), it is rendered stainless (vimalīkṛta).

It has been brought to a state of purity, its nature as the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of verbal expression having dissolved; for this very reason, it is "milked" by you yourself, who are praiseworthy for your skillful artistry—you have drawn it forth and brought it here. The secondary resonance (*anuraṇana*) of the word *haṃsa* is that a swan is clever at extracting milk from a mixture of milk and water. || 10 ||

And because you grant us such auspicious knowledge (śivajñāna), therefore, although there is a distinction in the delimitation of the six means of valid cognition (ṣaṭpramāṇī), [you remain] non-differentiated.
We offer this oblation to you, Bhava, for the sake of the single reality that is the ultimate truth.
It exists—*bhava*—because everything exists by way of the nature of the light of truth (*satyaprakāśātmanā rūpeṇa*).
For that very reason, it is of a single essential nature in the ultimate sense (*paramārthena*); to You, that *bhava*, we offer this oblation (*baliṃ yāmaḥ*).

To you alone, Bhairava-Agni, for whom the knowledge of Śiva has blossomed, we offer as an oblation our body, vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth. To what kind [of you]? To the one who possesses the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, postulation (*arthāpatti*), and non-existence (*abhāva*).

The aggregate of the six means of valid cognition (*ṣaṭpramāṇī*) is what is taught by the Mīmāṃsakas; the determination of each respective object produced by them is itself "differentiation"— consisting of the established arrangement of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) known as the perceptible and the imperceptible, similarity, sacrifice and its fruit, and the relationship between the goal and the means.
And it consists of the dependence upon the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; yet even when conjoined with these, it does not become divided, for its nature is such.
This is what is meant: whatever is established through various means of knowledge, because it is being so established, attains its status as an established entity only by resting upon consciousness.

Since everything consists of consciousness alone, even the establishment of duality is essentially Śiva, whose nature is the undivided Great Light; furthermore, the application of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and their objects of determination (*pariccheda*) can only be attributed to the Lord, because nothing exists apart from Him. Thus—
And even in the case of attribution (*saṃbhāvanā*), according to the view already stated, there is indeed non-difference. 11.

Thus, having attained immersion (*samāveśa*) through the offering of the *bali*, he speaks in order to express the hope that even during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) one may maintain that same nature:
"May we behold the profound..."
O Bhava, enter your own beautiful cave, which is entirely wiped clean of darkness by a supreme light. 12.

O Lord! [I enter] Your cave—the profound and endless power of Your Māyā—which has its inner and outer darkness wiped away on all sides by the supreme light, namely Your own non-dual radiance; for this very reason, it is beautiful.

Shining forth in its ultimate form as the essence of the power of absolute freedom—could we see, that is, could we enter into, that which is "within," namely, the state of identity with the subject within the self of the full I-consciousness? || 12 ||
Thus, with the intensity of devotion surging forth by the power of such aspiration, he said:
"Homage even to those who [possess] Soma— " (page 23)
They behold the Lord, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon and who bestows supreme bliss, even in their dreams.

Let alone the non-dual nature of the Supreme Lord, which provides consolation to the hearts of only a few; even for those who, at the very moment of seeing Him who possesses a physical form— the one whose crest is the moon—
experience supreme bliss even in a dream, [to them...]
Salutations to those who have been purified by the sight of you. || 13 ||
And since even these [gods] are to be saluted by us through the intensity of our devotion to you, therefore,
O Blessed One, [we offer] that which belongs to you.
To whom would a taste for cultivating existence not be pleasing— one that is skillful at cutting off the fear of rebirth? (14)
The inclination— the longing or faith— to contemplate, that is, to realize as one's own nature, that state which is your own essence, the mass of consciousness and bliss.
To whom would it not be pleasing? It means that it is evident to everyone. Of what nature is it?
It is capable—meaning empowered—in uprooting the fear of rebirth, that is, in eradicating the dread of future lives. || 14 ||
Therefore,
O Lord of the World, may this be our duty for as long as we live.
Through your grace, that state which arises from having a mind focused solely on you— || 15 ||

The meaning is: "By your grace alone, may not even a single moment be devoid of the contemplation of non-difference from you. "With you as the sole focus" (*tvadekāgra*) means one for whom you alone are the singular object to be constantly contemplated as the nature of one's own self. 15.
Furthermore, out of the excellence of his devotion, reflecting upon the unity of all scriptural statements,
he praises the nature of the Blessed One (page 25).
Salutations to you, whose self consists of the Vedas and Āgamas expanded across a thousand branches, and who brings forth infinite fruits.
To Śambhu, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree.

The Āgamas, which are of the nature of the Vedas according to the etymology "that by which one finds the supreme reality," are a single unified body of speech composed by the Supreme Lord; they are expanded into hundreds of different branches in accordance with the limited hearts of those who are attached to various specific portions [of truth]. Furthermore, likewise...

Every scripture has as its essence repose in the reality of the single supreme object; he whose self consists of that [scripture] is indeed the Supreme Lord himself, whose body is the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), manifesting through the nature of all scriptures which are the expansion of that [mass]. Therefore, it is "infinite"—unlimited, consisting of the manifestation of one's own essential nature—which is the fruit.
Upon its production—that is, its manifestation—it is like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛk�sa*), yielding fruit without delay;

for, according to the various branches imagined by the limited hearts [of individuals], it produces an infinite and manifold fruit. Yet, despite the difference in branches, the ritual action (*karman*) is one and the same, as it is to be understood through all the branches.
Thus, by means of this established principle and through a thorough consideration of the syntactic unity of the statements,
it is shown that there is indeed a resting in the ultimate fruit of one and the same [reality] which exists as the various scriptures.

Of this great treatise: as it has been stated in the *Sārasvata-stotra* regarding the various divergent systems—the three Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the doctrine of Paśupati, and that of Viṣṇu—each claiming, "This is the supreme one; that is the beneficial path."
Due to the diversity of inclinations among men who follow various straight and crooked paths, you alone are the goal for all, just as the ocean is for all waters.
Thus [ends the section]. 16.
Since this is so, therefore,
O Lord, having directed the actions of speech, mind, and body toward you;
Having become one with you, shall we too ever become free from the pairs of opposites? 17.

Whatever we speak, whatever we imagine, or whatever we do, we contemplate everything as being composed of You alone; therefore, through this state of being composed of You, we are free from dualities— meaning our sense of duality has dissolved—
and thus remain unassailed by all pairs of opposites such as pleasure and pain.
(27) Perhaps, at some time, we might even come to exist. || 17 ||
This hope of ours has indeed borne fruit, since the Blessed One is such;
with this intention, he utters a praise consisting of a reflection upon that extraordinary excellence:
"Of the worlds, [the Lord of] creation and destruction..."
Salutations to the wielder of the trident, whose power is independent of anything else, and who is the source of all those various beneficial injunctions. 18.

To the trident-bearer, for whom the expansion of the supreme power is definitively established, and who, from that very source, ordains welfare for all the worlds— from Sadāśiva down to the level of the Sakala— for their various births and dissolutions,
and for the attainment of their respective desired goals through the provision of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
"Salutation to the one whose nature is the unfolding of his own independent sovereignty, which is free from all dependence"—as before; likewise in what follows.
Or rather, enough with this excessive [praise] of Dhūrjaṭi, the primary object of meditation, whose possession of virtues has long since passed away.
For those who meditate even upon the Name through their meditations, what fruit could there be from other objects of focus? 19.

O Dhūrjaṭi—of Mahādeva—even a name such as "Dhūrjaṭi" and so forth, though devoid of the actual correspondence of meaning, yet when repeatedly contemplated as being grounded in the true reality (*tattvārtha*), what does it not produce?
Therefore, let that very [name] be contemplated. As he will say:
"O Lord, even Your name alone bestows the attainment of liberation as its ultimate fruit.
Likewise:
"By whose name alone great souls are covered with the sprouts of horripilation..."
Thus, since the mere contemplation of the Name itself nourishes the desired goal,
what purpose is served by other meditations (*dhyāna*) that have various forms as their objects? And it is said in the *Śrī-Vijñānabhairava*:
"Because he causes everything to resound out of fear, he is the giver of all and pervades the entire universe"— by the constant recitation of this word *Bhairava*, one becomes Śiva.
(Page 29) Thus:
"of the word" means [the focus is] on the word alone; for in reality, the word *bhairava* functions with the full meaning previously described.
Therefore, even without the contemplation of that meaning, whoever [continually...]

He who utters it becomes Śiva himself—just like the supreme mantra—because of the identity between the denoter and the denoted in the case of such [mantras] as the Bhagavān-mantra. Of what kind is Dhūrjaṭi? He is "beyond the connection with qualities," meaning that by virtue of being the nature of the Great Light free from the three guṇas, he is devoid of limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as form; for this very reason...
Of the primary object of meditation—that which is to be worshipped even by Brahmā and all other causes who themselves serve as objects of meditation. || 20 ||
Once again, his heart overflowing with the intensity of the weight of devotion, he spoke,
relying on the power of the mantra: "Obeisance, obeisance to Śiva!"
Blessed are those who are intent upon enjoying the prosperity of Śambhu. || 20 ||
To Śiva— for Him whose form is the singular mass of the supreme good consisting of consciousness and bliss— *namo namaḥ*, that is, repeatedly and without interruption.
In this manner, we offer as oblation the body, the vital breaths, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void, as well as the entire universe through those means;
thus, those who are established— that is, who have entered— into the true reality of that mantra’s majesty,
they are able to enjoy the Śāmbhava manifestation consisting of great bliss by way of non-difference from their own self.
Those who strive to produce wonder are praiseworthy. || 20 ||
Thinking "we too are such as that," he spoke thus out of pride within himself; or rather,
for us who possess intense devotion,
what path could there be that is not attainable?
And what speech is it that is not spoken by you?
What meditation is it by which you are not to be meditated upon?
Or what is it, O Lord, that you are not? (22)
What indeed is gained by this reference to mantras such as "Namo namaḥ śivāya"?

For whatever does not possess the nature of immeasurability and great luminosity (*amitattva-mahāprakāśa*), what is that? It is nothing at all. Therefore, what kind of path—what bodily sequence of action (*kāyīya-kriyākrama*)—could there be [for such a thing]?
(31) By which you are not attained; even all speech has you as its object. All meditation, consisting of mental volition, likewise has you as its sole support. And therefore, without effort—
We have always been born as one with you. || 21 ||
For this very reason, in all circumstances, one thinks:
"This one has been honored; this one has been meditated upon; this one has been gratified."
May my essence increase within you through a thousand channels. || 22 ||

Since everything belonging to me— through all the activities of body, mind, and speech— rests solely upon the Blessed One, therefore this Blessed One, whose ultimate reality is consciousness and who manifests in all states as "this" and "that," is worshipped, meditated upon, and fully gratified in due order; such is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
May that attachment of mine toward you, which has taken root, flourish with a hundred branches. || 22 ||
And therefore:
Homage to the one whose intellect is like a leaf that has shed all [impurities]— (page 32)
To you, the Lord Sthāṇu, whose nature consists of garlands and abodes, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread— salutations!
Salutations to you, Sthāṇu—the one whose single form is indestructible. To what kind [of being]?

To him who has the serpent Vāsuki as his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Thus, even though you possess such a physical form, it is a marvel that you are seen in various ways, whether appearing in a painting or even within the realm of one's desires.
O Protector, you bestow the perfect fruit of the ultimate truth.

Thus, by way of this state of being, he says that the Blessed Lord is indeed full: "of all"—from Śiva down to an insect—"and of all" those cognitions or consciousnesses, which, due to their flickering nature, are like rows of birds; the dissolution (*laya*) of these—

To him whose self rests in the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) and whose very nature consists of that—[the world] becomes like a withered tree (*sthāṇu*), resembling an old tree, inhabited by flocks of birds. || 23 ||
He states this prayer, which is worthy of homage, [beginning with]: "The sole [remedy] for the darkness of ignorance... (page 33).
Your remembrance is the medicine;
O Bhava, by granting me those various [remedies],
please show me your grace.
Ignorance is precisely the non-manifestation of identity with Śiva; blindness is the defect that displays duality by obstructing the eye of supreme intuition.
Your remembrance alone, which consists of the reflective awareness of your own nature as the mass of consciousness, is the sole medicine—the means for its pacification.
Therefore, by granting that—that is, by bringing about a state of one-pointed absorption—let grace be bestowed;
let purity be attained through the quieting of the turbidity of non-apprehension (akhyāti). || 24 ||
Once again, overcome by the weight of devotion, he offers this hymn of praise, appropriate for the expectation of his grace:
"Obeisance to the Lord, the accomplisher of all human goals in their entirety."
Even a prostration made to him is worthy of being offered by the wise in this world. (25)

Even the salutation of the wise— those who know reality— which consists of the aforementioned immersion (*samāveśa*), [is sufficient] for the entirety of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), namely both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).

Because He is the accomplisher and likewise the ornament, He is to be saluted—He is to be resorted to with humility; again and again, let there be *namaḥ* to that Lord, who possesses such extraordinary sovereignty. || 25 ||
And this is fitting:
for those submerged in the terrible ocean of existence, the abode of the sea-monsters of suffering.
Having then obtained the *Śārva-bhakticintāmaṇi* (the wish-fulfilling gem of devotion to Śiva), what has not been conquered? || 26 ||

In the ocean of saṃsāra, which consists of afflictions difficult to cross, the "sea-monsters" (*yādāṃsi*) are the sufferings— the torments arising from external elements and so forth— such as the *makara* and others; by those who are submerged, that is, completely drowned, in that very place, the abode of those monsters, [they attain] the state of Śarva.
By His very will, [he attained] the *bhakticintāmaṇi* (the wish-fulfilling jewel of devotion) belonging to Śarva, the supreme refuge of the universe.
(Page 35)

"Having obtained"—meaning having attained quite suddenly—what is it that has not been conquered, i.e., not overcome, such as the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth? And what is it that has not been conquered, i.e., not attained, such as enjoyments (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*)? The meaning is that everything desired is indeed obtained instantaneously. And thus, [it is said] regarding Nandi, Mahākāla, and others:
The attainment of various desired objects is heard of in the Āgamas. || 26 ||
And devotion alone is the cause for the thorough knowledge of the true nature of the Lord, and nothing else; thus he says:
"Of those possessing the wealth of unobstructed, non-dual, and unwavering knowledge..."
"O Dhūrjaṭi, it is said that those who know you are indeed some extraordinary beings. (27)
"Kila" means "according to tradition"— thus it is said indeed in the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*). From "obscuration"—

meaning those from whom the wealth of knowledge has emerged, which consists of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), is free from duality, takes the form of supreme non-duality (*paramādvaita*), and is unwavering and unshakable— it is for them alone, O Dhūrjaṭi, that you become the object of knowledge.
You manifest as self-luminous; therefore, these few individuals— these very extraordinary great souls— are indeed those who perceive You as manifesting in non-difference from themselves.
They recognize [it]. || 27 ||
And therefore,
though devoid of qualities, the one unborn Lord, as the knower of qualities, triumphs as the sole object of knowledge for those who possess such knowledge.
Even though he is by nature free from desire, he is the supreme fruit of all desires.
He who illuminates the qualities consisting of the aforementioned knowledge is one—without a second—and unborn—beginningless;

though devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), meaning his form is untouched by qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, he is "knowable"—capable of being known—as he flashes forth in non-difference from oneself. Likewise, because he is filled with perfect bliss, [he is the source] of desires...
Although he has emerged from desires, by his very nature— through the inherent beauty of reality—

he is the supreme, that is, the full, fruit of all desires; for while all desires are indeed joined with fruits consisting of various enjoyments, they are nonetheless preceded by the wonder of the subject who enjoys.
They culminate in the ocean of ultimate, final bliss. As it has been said by our venerable masters (p.
"The fruit of ritual actions or of injunctions..."
But in the final analysis, O Lord, there is only identity with You;
for those who, however, desire a fruit here,
their state would be that of fools, characterized by instability alone.
Thus [it is said]. The two words "api" (even/also) indicate a contradiction. || 28 ||
This too is an extraordinary excellence unique to the Blessed One; thus he says:
"In this [teaching], which gods have not exerted themselves for the sake of attaining the nectar of the jewel of glory?"
O All-pervading Lord, that sovereignty over the ocean of milk is indeed innate to you alone.

In that Ocean of Milk— where, for the sake of obtaining Lakṣmī, the Kaustubha gem, the Pārijāta tree, and other jewels, as well as the nectar of immortality, which gods such as Upendra and others did not suffer? That is to say, by all of them, great hardship was endured— for such a treasure-trove of wonders as that Ocean of Milk.
O All-pervading Lord! Sovereignty is yours alone by nature; for another, however, it cannot be attained even through thousands of acts of worship.
It is not something to be acquired, since it was already bestowed by you upon the sage Upamanyu from the Ocean of Milk. || 29 ||
Therefore,
O Bhava, salutations to you with devotion; for those who seek liberation, you become the protector of men.
Through mindfulness and praise, one bestows auspiciousness upon Śambhu in existence and non-existence.
O Bhava! Salutations to you, Śambhu. To what kind of one?

To him who manifests for the liberation of men characterized by devotion—that is, as the nature of liberation consisting of identity with his own expansion—and likewise to him who protects those characterized by remembrance, guarding them from all fears.

Thus, by means of praise (*nuti*)—that is, through the cause of hymn (*stuti*)—they bestow upon [the devotees] in *bhava* (saṃsāra) auspiciousness (*śam*), which consists of the excellence of enjoyments, just as [He did] for Upamanyu, Marutta, and others; and in *abhava* (liberation), they grant that which has liberation as its ultimate goal. This is the meaning. || 30 ||

Not only is the desired goal accomplished by you for those seeking liberation, for the afflicted, and for those desiring worldly enjoyment, but even the desire for liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is fulfilled; thus he says:
O Lord, for those endowed with the knowledge that "I am omniscient, the doer of all, and everything," what object of knowledge or action could there be?
But it is not offered by you for the sake of infinity. || 31 ||

"You alone are the omniscient one, whose very nature is that of the creator of all; you are the conscious self (cidātman), and you are everything. For those who shine with such knowledge, what object of cognition—whether it be that which is to be known, action, or that which is to be performed in the form of activity—is there that is not offered by you for infinity? Indeed, everything is so offered.

The meaning is that these are shown as having the nature of the All (vaiśvātmya). And thus, everywhere, the manifestation of the sovereignty of Maheśvara, which consists of all things, is liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 31 ||
Enough with the limitation of the Lord’s favors, since such is the extent of His very will.
The fruit consists of the three worlds; O Lord, who knows the extent of the course of those deeds of Yours? (32)

Who knows the extent—the limit or the range—of the effects, that is, the things brought about by effort, of Him who by mere will ordains the three worlds consisting of existence, non-existence, and super-existence? No one knows it; this is truly inconceivable.

This is intended solely as a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*); there is nothing whatsoever that must be accomplished by the Blessed One’s effort. Here, the meaning of the sentence functions as the object (*karman*), just as in the expression "the deer runs. 32.

Not only is the vast extent of your activity impossible to know, but even the greatness of your knowledge consisting of sovereign power is so; thus he says: "Even Brahmā and the others [cannot know] that of yours."
By means of the stairway of karma,
they run higher and higher to attain the unmeasured abode; to Him I bow.

In order to attain that inconceivable abode— the state of Brahman, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the rest— by means of the stairway of karma, that is, through the succession of practices such as meditation upon each of them;

"Higher and higher"—thus they run with an ever-increasing intensity of effort and a desire for greater excellence, yet they find no rest whatsoever. For in the state of the Supreme Lord, which is the universal totality (*sarvasāmānya*), there is no possibility of connection with either superiority or inferiority; how then can that [state] be sought by those who desire ever-increasing excellence?
"It is attained"—thus, even the greatness of this knowledge belonging to Maheśvara is indeed immeasurable. || 33 ||
Moreover, these manifestations are due to His very power; thus he says:
"This is Brahmā, this is Mahendra, and these two are the Sun and the Moon."
May that Bhava protect you, whose creeper of power has thus blossomed. || 34 ||
The term "this Brahmā" refers to Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva; by this, it denotes those who perform their respective functions, such as creation and maintenance.
Brahmā and the others, as well as Mahendra who stands in the sovereignty over the gods, and the sun and moon who exist as the performers of the world's functions such as illumination and nourishment—
whatever else of this kind exists, endowed with great majesty, all that belongs to Him.

Śakti—whose nature is capacity—is like a creeper; she is "flowered," meaning she has blossomed merely by the appearance of flowers but has not yet borne fruit. For everything that is like a flower, the attainment of non-difference from the Supreme Lord is itself the fruit, consisting of supramundane wonder. As it is said in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra:
"In the discussion on immersion (*samāveśa*),

no distinction in the fruit of consciousness (*saṃvitti*) should be postulated here by the wise. And he for whom the creeper of power (*śakti-latā*) has thus blossomed is *bhava*, whose true nature (*satattva*) has been explained previously.

May they protect— may they guard me— from this association with the mental resolve for the worship of Brahmā and others; and may the omniscient lords of the worlds, beginning with Brahmā, who are the creators of all, be praised by me.
We praise that auspicious Śiva, the ocean of awakening, wherein these [phenomena] bubble forth like bubbles.
Thus [ends the section]. 34.
(43) Thus, in this manner, no error is found for that which is all-pervasive.
We praise that Mṛḍa, whose limit is inaccessible even to those with deluded internal organs and even to those who have gone far away. 35.
We praise—that is, we fully enter—that Maheśvara, who is Mṛḍa, consisting of supreme bliss.

Of what nature is he? He whom those with deluded internal organs—even while searching for a long time through the excellence of yoga consisting of the meditation on His supreme greatness—[only encounter] delusion.

No limit can be found; likewise, even by those who have traveled far—by those proceeding through the stages of cultivation over an exceedingly remote path—the end, which is the completion of its length, and the temporal limits of its beginning and end cannot be found, because it is formless and thus devoid of spatial and temporal connection. Therefore...
Thus, those whose internal faculties are deluded are described as being intent on searching for the Blessed One by means of his physical form.
Furthermore, even at the time of dissolution, when he manifests in the midst of the waters in the form of flames according to his own will,
[those such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu] fail to perceive his true majesty because they do not contemplate his essential greatness.
(Page 44) Since those with deluded minds, though searching, did not obtain a definitive determination,
this also touches upon the traditional meaning. Furthermore, for one whose very confusion is related [to it]...
The Great Māyā-ātman is not found—it is not delimited.

For indeed, all [deities] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are deluded by Māyā; therefore it is said that they possess deluded internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Where even this power of His Māyā is not found—it is not delimited—[there He resides].

In that regard, how could he be delimited? Even by those who are far removed—even by Anāśrita and the others who have ascended the stream of the six paths—the limit of whom is difficult to discern is simply not found. || 35 ||

With the intention that one who possesses devotion is, in all states, composed solely of the firm support of non-difference from the Blessed One, he says: "Salutation in praise, remembrance, and meditation."
To the beloved Kapardin, for the sake of a multitude of joys upon seeing, touching, and attaining him.

Salutation to Kapardin, to Mahādeva; salutation to Dayita, the most beloved. Of what nature is he? In praise—namely, in the utterance of his name; in remembrance—namely, in the contemplation of his meaning.

In *dhyāna*—in meditation, which is one-pointedness of mind upon the Self; in *darśana*—in the direct perception that arises immediately thereafter; in *sparśana*—in resting therein; and in *prāpti*—in attaining identity with That; or else, since everything consists of the Blessed One, [this occurs] at all times within the functions of all the senses.

And in the attainment whose nature is repose in one's own essential form, [it leads] to a multitude of blisses—that is, to the expansion of supreme joy. Even a worldly beloved brings progressively greater happiness through the sequence beginning with praise and ending with union; however, the Supreme Lord does so in every respect.
"Consisting solely of perfect bliss, neither deficient nor excessive"— this is the *vyatirekadhvani* (suggestive power based on exclusion) rooted in the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*).
And since, in all states, there shines forth only the nature of the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) who consists of a multitude of blisses, therefore...
O Supreme Lord, even though he thought in his mind, "What is the use of pride?",
he nonetheless felt pride [thinking], "I am identical with You."
Why are you so joyful regarding me and not regarding yourself? || 37 ||
(Page 46) Even regarding the status of Brahmā and others who perform various acts of creation and so forth— which is perishable— whatever pride or arrogance (*smaya*) there may be,
having thought and even ascertained in one's mind that "by that, nothing [is gained]," O Supreme Lord—

O You who transcend all, by means of that joy (*mud*)— which is the Great Egoity (*mahābhimāna*) consisting of the smile [arising from the thought] "I am composed of You," which blossoms through the power of the recognition of Your true nature— do I not abide in this very Self? That is to say,
do I not indeed manifest as the Fullness itself?

Or rather, even while abandoning all forms of self-conceit, how was it that out of joy produced by the pride [of thinking] "I am absorbed in You," he acted in such a way that he did not abide—did not remain—within his own self? || 37 ||
"Even with such a conceit, I find my rest in you alone," he says:
"For even after reflecting, there are millions of things to be done due to the fickleness of the mind."
Resting in this state, O Bhava, may I take great delight in the bliss of your consciousness.
(47) Due to this natural restlessness of the mind, [one thinks]: "Today I have obtained this; I shall attain that desire."
I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice.
Having reflected upon— and indeed having mentally resolved upon— these successions of duties that proceed without interruption,
cognitive power (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) are clearly established for every living being, precisely because they manifest as the appearance of whatever is intended.

Thus, according to the direction of the reflection upon the reality of the object as determined by *pratyabhijñā* (recognition): O Bhava, within the bliss of Your consciousness—Your very consciousness being the perfect bliss—I, resting therein, rejoice intensely; even the entire universe, extending to its outermost limits, is indeed drenched in the essence of Your bliss.
He remains established in experience. As it is said in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"For one who fully recognizes, 'All this is my own manifestation,' there is the state of the Great Lord even amidst the proliferation of mental constructs regarding the universal self."

Thus, the means for entering the supreme reality (*paratattva*) which was described in the first verse by way of pacifying the mind consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is an even more excellent means: even during emergence (*vyutthāna*),
it is entirely saturated with the essence of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

The intention behind the statement "he acts" and "I rejoice intensely" is that this means [of attainment] takes root solely through the sequence of its specific means; thus it has been stated here by the author of the hymn in that very order.
The state of being conscious is *cittatā*; *cintā* is a corrupt reading. || 38 ||
And even when investigated in this manner, [the Self] does not become an object of knowledge; thus he says:
"If you are subtle, how can these three worlds be but a mere fraction of you?"
O Lord, is that which is gross not easily perceived even by Brahmā and the other gods? (39)

Regarding that which was previously stated in the verse beginning with "praṇavordhvārdhamātrāta"— the reality therein is this: that the Supreme Lord is of the singular nature of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*).

It never becomes an object of cognition; otherwise, how could this triple world—consisting of non-existence, existence, and the state beyond existence—be even a mere fraction of that which is of the nature of the absolute atom?
For if it were gross, it could not be encompassed by those beginning with Brahmā and ending with Śiva.
It would be difficult to perceive; they would apprehend it solely through sensory perception,
rather than being anxious seekers after it, because it is entirely impossible to delimit.
The Supreme Lord is the single embodiment of consciousness, whose nature is everything and who consists of everything; therefore, all scriptures are firmly established in Him alone.
Thus, we who are devoted to His investigation are indeed acting appropriately. 39.
Otherwise,
if this [teaching] had not existed, you yourself would have been the one to whom these [doctrines] were to be proclaimed.
O King, who that is truly wise would then have allowed himself to be entangled in the web of words regarding affliction? (40)

The waves of the scriptures, which are nets of speech, appear as if they were concealing Your true essential nature; yet in reality, because they consist of the body of the aggregate of sounds, they rest precisely within Your true essential nature. Therefore, if this were not so—no.

Since it will be recognized [as such], what wise person—meaning, one who follows authoritative means of knowledge—would apply himself to this investigation, which yields nothing but exhaustion? || 40 ||

(50) Although you are in reality identical with the universe, nevertheless, may you grant me grace through this instruction that brings about the direct realization of your true nature— may you bestow upon me purity— for this reason:

Without your grace, you cannot be directly realized by anyone through any sequence of practices such as meditation (*dhyāna*) or concentration (*dhāraṇā*), nor by any intellect characterized by sharp discernment; on the contrary,
it is only upon the total subsiding of all activity and cognition that your true nature shines forth.
"This dissolution of that [state] has been previously described; let grace be bestowed.
Thus he spoke in sequence: "By what action or by what wisdom, O Lord?"
By the instruction "you are visible," please grant me grace. || 41 ||
This is clear. || 41 ||

Thus, even after such a prayer, one who has attained direct realization of that [Reality] speaks in order to praise its true nature— even during the state of emergence— as it is colored by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) thereof (page 51).
Homage to the one who requires no assistance,
the sole benefactor of the three worlds,
who is desirable to all.
To the one who is free from desire, the one with matted hair.
Because there is no benefactor or benefit distinct [from the Self], it is for the one who has nothing to be benefited—that is, for the one who cannot be assisted;

and for that very reason, because there is nothing desirable, it is for the one who is free from desire (*niḥspṛha*); for *kapardin*, meaning "one with matted hair"—this designation is employed here as being appropriate to his state of desirelessness. Thus, it is for the one who cannot be benefited.

And to you alone— who, though free from desire for anything, act as the sole benefactor of the three worlds by fulfilling all that is desired, and who are therefore worthy of longing— since you have favored us by bringing about the purification of our own nature without any motive whatsoever, we offer our bodies and all else. Thus [he says].
The Blessed One is said to possess supramundane excellence. || 42 ||
Thus, praising himself as one filled with devotion through these general words, he says (on page 52):
"Oh, how wonderful is this state of being a knower of the field!"
O Lord, by means of this [devotion], these virtuous ones sow devotion unto You, which yields infinite fruit, for the sake of the great goal of the righteous.

O Master, for the virtuous—those who have been graced by you—oh, what a marvel! This is their state of being the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajñatā), that is, their state of being the Puruṣa. Moreover, this very state of being the Knower of the Field—their awareness and cognition directed toward You, the Field, who are the cause of protection from all afflictions and the cycle of transmigration—is realized within their own selves.

Having realized Your power— for the sake of the great purpose which is non-difference from You— by means of that state of being the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajñatā), these virtuous ones plant devotion— that is, service— in You, the Field, by abandoning the desire for separate fruits, and thus cause it to sprout like a seed.
What kind of devotion?—That which has as its fruit the attainment of identity with You, arising simply from sowing in Your field; [it is] "infinite," meaning unconditioned. || 43 ||
Thus, those who do not take root in such devotion— which leads to the attainment of the treasure that is your true nature— are utterly deluded by your own māyā.
Thus he said:
"O Illusionist, alas, this great illusion of yours remains unperceived by me!"
Even upon obtaining the treasure-trove of meditation upon you,
the deluded world grows lax.
"Mahatī" means difficult to transcend; "māyā" is non-apprehension (akhyāti); "māyin" refers to one intent on concealing his own true nature.

By this [māyā], whose essential reality is the concealment of one's own nature, the deluded person—whose vision of reality is obscured and covered, and who lacks discernment regarding the truth—becomes slack; that is, even when devotion to You is attained, he does not become absorbed in You.
Thus, he says that you alone are the agent in all cases: "In every undertaking, whether it be the object, or the action, or the instrument and so forth, be present."
May the universe be independent; you alone shall be its sole creator therein.

(54) O Lord, in every undertaking— that is, in every activity pertaining to subjects ranging from Śiva down to an insect— whatever appears as if it were of the nature of an agent, an instrument, and so forth, all that is indeed the object (*karman*).

Let the effect (*kārya*) be that which is manifested as such through the act (*kriyā*), whose nature is manifestation, belonging to you alone as the independent agent (*kartṛ*). Or rather, let it be the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, since it is manifested by you yourself as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for a limited action; however, in all these cases here—

Even though You alone manifest as the manifold variety of diverse forms, You are the one, independent, and autonomous agent; others, however, being merely manifestations of You, are not autonomous—how then could they be agents? As for the agency attributed to Brahmā and others at the time of creation and so forth, that belongs to them [only]...

Its true nature consists merely in the various respective notions (abhimāna) awakened by you. As it was stated by the venerable Vidyādhipati: "For one who perceives a higher state through successive stages of comprehension, that which is lower is [sublated] by the higher."
In this case, the cause for you is the grasping at your own mental projections regarding the means of accomplishment, which are like mirages.
Thus [ends the section]. || 45 ||
Since this is so, therefore:
[the state] characterized by the three qualities and the threefold vibration—
The three worlds are seized by the pairs of opposites;
who other than you has the power or the compassion to uplift them? (46)

By means of those pairs of opposites— cold and heat, hunger and thirst, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion, birth and death— which consist of the threefold activity (parispanda) characterized by manifestation, engagement, and persistence, belonging to the three qualities (guṇas) beginning with sattva, and which reside in the body, the vital breath, and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka).

"Devoured"—meaning made one's own—is the triple world, the cycle of living beings encompassed by the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; "to uplift it" means to cause it to take hold of the state that is beyond the fourth (turyātīta). It is your power alone, O Teacher, which manifests your majesty upon the levels of the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and so forth.
Whether it be capacity or compassion—whose nature is the desire to favor—it belongs to no one else at any time.
As it has been said:
"Abiding in the body of the teacher, Śiva cuts away the bonds."
Thus:
one hundred and eighteen. (Page 56) —————— One hundred and eighteen.
Having personally favored him, Śiva appointed him to the office of Lord of Mantras.
Thus [ends the verse]. 46.
Thus, he says that the very presence or absence of the contemplation of oneness with you constitutes virtue and fault:
"O Lord, even a fault— what fault is there—
for one who has set out to attain you?"
Moreover, what quality indeed, even if it were a quality, would not strive to attain you? (47)
O Lord, even one who is intent on various worldly diversions and possesses thirst for sense objects is truly endowed with virtue if he consists of the contemplation of You alone; whereas one who,
though possessed of virtues such as scholarship and dispassion, lacks the essence of contemplation upon You, is indeed flawed.

He is one whose wisdom is truly pitiable; "firmly established" means he stands completely and correctly through non-differentiation—that is, he is deeply attached [to the notion of difference]. || 47 ||
And for this reason,
O Lord of the World, let there also be passion.
Salutations to that very greed which resides in you alone, for it is my support for attaining you. (47)

"In you alone," meaning not in both you and the fruit. By the word "namas" (salutation), he confirms the very intensity of devotion to the Blessed One. *Rāga* is longing; *lobha* is guarding [you] as if you were one's own life; *tvallābha* is immersion in you;
and *ālambana* is that which has you as its object. || 47 ||
"One whose nature is characterized by such passion and greed is uplifted by the contemplation of You"—thus he says:
"Aho! Great indeed is this deed, O Lord, which consists of the contemplation of You."
From Brahmā down to a worm, who among us would not be qualified for liberation? (48)
(Page 58) In rites consisting of Vedic meditations (*bhāvanā*) such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which bestow heaven, only the twice-born (*dvija*) is authorized; however,
in rites consisting of meditations upon You, everyone from Prajāpati down to a mere worm is so authorized.

"By Your will alone, the universe has been made fit for liberation"— by thus manifesting His unimpeded sovereignty through the power of the meaning (*arthaśakti*) via a suggestion of contrast (*vyatirekadhvani*), the Lord suggests the sentiment of wonder (*adbhutarasa*). || 48 ||
Moreover,
the undertaking is the beginning of all tasks, and the completion is the end of all actions.
O Lord, the various mental states occurring within that [intellect] are on the very path of Your own consciousness.

He is the Lord, the independent one; through his own consciousness alone, he knows the beginning, middle, and end of all effects—such as worldly enjoyment and liberation—as well as their respective activities. || 49 ||
Although your consciousness illumines the entire universe, nevertheless,
there is a certain greatness in devotion as it is thus illumined; so he says:
Up to the highest [level], it expands a thousandfold in its savor—
the nectar of the rasa of devotion to you.
O Lord, it is not seen anywhere else. || 50 ||

O Lord— whose very nature is to be prayed to— whatever is higher and higher, as far as the highest reaches, that essence of immersion which is the flavor of devotion to You is indeed nectar because it consists of supreme bliss; elsewhere, nowhere else, is there anything higher than this, step by step, in terms of the various tastes.
A thousandfold—that is, innumerable—expansion of wonders, which are clusters of bliss, is seen; devotion to you alone bestows ever-increasingly superior riches of supreme bliss.
"Āsvādya" is a corrupt reading. Regarding the word "vistara," one must consider that this is a term used for something beyond the scope of words.
Since it is thus with respect to extension (*prathana*) and not sound (*śabda*), therefore...
To him who has withdrawn all desires,
who does not extend the prospect of further desires,
and who has the moon as his crest-ornament.
Salutation to Soma, the Master. || 51 ||
The Lord— the Great Lord whose nature is consciousness— who exists together with the Goddess Umā, that is, his own power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*),
is one who has united all immeasurable moons within his own supreme head, which is the form of the Supreme Power. Therefore,
because there is no object to be sought as something external, he has withdrawn all desire into himself alone, in close proximity (*upa*).

To him who is eternally satisfied by the wonder of his own bliss, and who, precisely because of that perfection, perpetually manifests within himself all future expansion— the manifold variety of forms and actions— to him, [I offer] salutation; such is the meaning according to the internal sequence.
But externally, for the sake of subduing passion, [he considers] the future, the auspicious time to come,
when [the teaching] will proceed eternally in places such as Kailāsa.
(Page 61)

The meaning is: "Salutation to the one who possesses supramundane power consisting of play filled with intense joy, who bears half of Umā’s body, and who wears the crescent moon as an ornament—even though he is the burner of Manmatha.
And also [to the one] who burns the god of love...

"Being established in a universal erotic sentiment (*sāmānya-śṛṅgāra*) that is complete with the objective support (*ālambana*), the inflaming factors (*uddīpana*), and the transitory moods (*vibhāva*)," thus,

even while possessing a formal structure, an exceedingly difficult-to-achieve sovereignty has been described. And yet, [those who are] devoted have been brought to completion through the manifestation of the full nature [of the Lord].

"By whom all desires—longings—have been pacified, and for that very reason, by whom the future of desire has not been extended—that is, who at all times displays the nature of being embraced by the Fortune of Liberation—to that Lord, obeisance.
This also is its meaning. || 51 ||
Thus, for the time being, I am indeed intent on protecting my devotion and my wealth; nevertheless,
if your sovereign power of illusion (māyā-śakti) causes me— who have forgotten my true nature— to fall into its midst, what can I do, being powerless?
For one who does not form any attachment anywhere,
may the power of Śaṅkara, which bestows grace upon all, be my refuge. 52.

(Page 62) Due to being deluded by some power of illusion belonging to the Great Lord who consists of play, during the state of emergence, he is incapable [of acting] and thinks everywhere: "What am I to do? Nothing at all."
For me, who— by the command of the Supreme Lord— am utterly bewildered (*kāndiśīka*) because I do not resolve upon nor grasp any determination regarding the activities of body, mind, or speech,
there exists the power belonging to Śaṅkara, which brings about the welfare consisting of the manifestation of supreme non-duality.
The meaning is: she alone, whose sole purpose is the welfare of all, is my refuge; she herself will awaken me once again. || 52 ||
Nor should it be said that while Śaṅkara has solely the purpose of bestowing grace, there might be some other Lord who is a deluder;
for [it is stated] of him who has transcended the qualities (guṇas):
O Bhava, where in this world can a supreme substitute be found for you, whose nature consists of excellence beyond all measure?

(Page 63) He remains eternally established in a form whose sole essence is the manifestation of existence; yet, due to the association with the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, multiplicity arises for those subjects under the influence of *māyā*. You, however, transcend these qualities.
"You are the singular embodiment of independent consciousness. For one such as you, who could be even a mere fraction—a counterpart or equal?
Since there is no possible differentiator of consciousness whatsoever, how could there be any suspicion of a rival lord? It is for this very reason that you are the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
[He is] the independent agent therein, you alone;
thus, by such [statements], he is one whose nature consists of every excellence without exception, whose essence is established as possessing all preeminence.
In the reading *nirmṛṣṭa*, it means one who has completely polished away all [other] excellences.
The construction should be understood as: "one whose self (ātman) has the form of nothing but the single great universal consciousness. || 53 ||
Therefore, even though you are the sovereign Lord, when we are deluded by your own *māyā* during occasional emergence from that state,
we cry out to you alone as our savior for the sake of your manifestation— just as it was said regarding that which is free from duality and free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhi*).
O Lord, even though You are our very Self,
we are still deceived today by Your unfathomable māyā.

"O Lord, you who are affectionate toward your servants, O Great God, who are free from dualities, whose nature is supreme non-duality, and who have likewise transcended the limiting conditions of place, time, and form— yet not [otherwise]..."

Even though the Self has been established as such by determining it to be of the nature of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) and so forth, we— even having ascended to such a stream of awakening— up to this day are still deceived by Your sovereign, immeasurable Māyā; [we are deceived] not even slightly by the latent impression (saṃskāra) of identifying with the body as the knower.

We abandon it; therefore, O Lord, this task is known only to You—act in such a way that even this residual impression of *māyā* is pacified for us, Your servants. Thus it was said by me as well in my hymn of praise (*svastotra*).
Though uprooted a hundred times and crushed a thousand times, the power of devotion to the Lord of Cows (Kṛṣṇa) rises up again instantly; here, Śiva is the refuge.
Thus [ends the verse]. 54.
And this pacification is not difficult to attain,
since it results in the acquisition of qualities such as atomization (aṇimā), eternal sovereignty, and the destruction of worldly existence.
