These are the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree of devotion to You, O Bhava. || 55 ||

(65) The attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* by Brahmā and others, the eternal sovereignty of Sadāśiva and others, and the destruction of worldly existence for pure souls— these are but the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree that is devotion to you, and not [the fruit].

Whether it be flowers or fruits— since its flower consists of the power of your skin (the Śakti) and its fruit is indeed your very self, and since the destruction of worldly existence is the sprout of devotion to you— therefore,
by your grace, the latent impression of Māyā must necessarily [cease] for us who partake in devotion to you.
The remaining intention is that [the world] will perish. And it is said in the *Vijñānabhairava*:

"The kind of realization that arises in one who is detached due to the intensity of devotion—that is the eternal power of Śaṅkara; therefore, one should contemplate that, and thereby one becomes Śiva."
Thus [ends the verse]. 55.
Thus, inflamed by the surging tide of devotion and aspiring for nothing less than total identity with Maheśvara— wherein all residual impressions of the body have dissolved— he says:
"In whichever direction one looks, there you are not."
"Every moment consists of you;
O Lord, tell me, when will I obtain You, even though You have already been obtained? (56)

That which is pointed out is *dik* (direction), that is, *deśa* (space); whatever *deśa* there may be whose nature is form, or *kāla* (time) whose nature is action— all of that, although established by this principle that because it is an object of cognition (*cetyamānatvāt*), it is essentially nothing but consciousness (*cidekātmaiva*)— is [so understood].

"O Lord, Master, although You consist of the universe, when—on what occasion—will You be attained? When shall we obtain Your true self-nature, free from the obstacle of even the slightest trace of the latent impressions of the subtle body? Please grant this command to Your servants. Thus [he spoke].
An expression full of affection born from deep intimacy. || 56 ||
Furthermore, with a weight of devotion, he says "Salutation" (namaḥ) in order to pay homage to Him who is the sole dwelling place for a mind characterized by serene and virtuous conduct.
To Śambhu, the Great Swan, whose body is whitened by abundant ashes; || 57 ||

"Salutation to Śambhu, the Great Haṃsa. The state of being a *haṃsa* is as previously described; however, his "greatness" (*mahattva*) is in relation to all the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls) and Rudras. For all subjects (*pramātāraḥ*) are indeed *haṃsas*, because they possess the nature of abandoning and assuming [states] consisting of their own appropriate emanation and withdrawal. But Śambhu...
He who effects the creation and dissolution even of them is the Mahāhaṃsa. For this very reason, it is said in the Śrī Svacchanda:
Having begun with "Śiva by means of Dharma is Haṃsa," it continues:
"The Self, indeed, is Haṃsa."

Thus it has been said. To what kind of Śambhu? To him in whom dwells the mind—the consciousness—of those of virtuous conduct, that is, those whose noble behavior consists of meditation upon you; a mind which, through the weight of devotion to you, is serene and free from doubt regarding the ultimate reality. In him alone does it reside.

To him who manifests by his very nature through the concealment of his own essence; likewise, to him whose limbs— meaning whose essential form consisting of the powers of knowledge and action— are bound (*sita*) by *bhūti*, which is abundant (*bhūri*), great, and consists of the manifold variety of the universe, namely *māyā*.
And the great swan, dwelling in the lake called Prasannamānasa, becomes white-bodied like abundant ash; such is the meaning of the resonance (anuraṇana). || 57 ||
And therefore,
with the darkness and exhaustion removed from the heart, and all the fuel of existence consumed, [the fire of knowledge blazes].
O Lord, may your lamp of awakening be mine, and may your lamp of devotion be mine.
"O Lord, let devotion to you alone be the lamp-flame, because it is illuminating; let it be the torch for your awakening—that is, the manifestor of your great light. Of what nature is it?"
By that [wisdom] which has removed and uprooted the exhaustion of darkness—
the torment of non-recognition— and by which the entire fuel of existence— the wood of *saṃsāra*— has been scorched and consumed; just as the flame of a lamp,
having dispelled the exhaustion of darkness in the form of soot yet not burning the entire wick, illuminates jars and other objects, therefore...
"This lamp of your awakening is indeed unique"—this is the figure of speech known as *vyatireka* (contrast). || 58 ||
Reflecting upon it through another form, he says:
"The drama of the three worlds contains within its womb many true seeds that have been cast forth."
Having introduced this subject, who else but you, O Hara, is capable of composing [this] poem? (59)
He is Hara, intent upon the destruction of the universe; the three worlds— consisting of existence, non-existence, and supreme existence—
he [perceives] through the application of various attributes such as the vocal, the physical, the artificial, and the involuntary (sāttvika).

Nāṭakamitra—having introduced and commenced [the topic] as if it were a drama to be performed, who other than you is capable of concluding—that is, of bringing it to rest—the poet, meaning the Creator? None at all, is the sense. Of what sort [is this world]? It has been emitted—produced—as manifold through the reality (*sattva*) of the virtuous.

The seed of the entities being displayed— namely *māyā*, *prakṛti*, and so forth— is within its womb, that is, inside it. And having introduced the specific type of poetry called a drama (*nāṭaka*) through the prologue (*prastāvanā*) by means of the opening juncture (*mukhasandhi*), one should conclude it by means of the concluding juncture (*nirvahaṇasandhi*).
Only a certain poet who has ascended to the heights of mastery is capable of composing a drama, not just anyone;
as they say:
"A drama should have a well-known plot... [and so forth].

Thus [it is asked]: what kind of drama is it? It is one in which the seed (*bīja*) and other elements, along with their connections, are released and established within the various junctures (*sandhi*). In the *garbha* (embryo) juncture, the purposes and so forth—such as the attainment of a kingdom—are deposited. As it has been said: [The text continues: "In which juncture, of which [element]... [and so on], up to "...the *garbha*, *avamarśa*, and *nirvahaṇa* [junctures]. The purposes and so forth, such as the acquisition of sovereignty, are placed within the *garbha* juncture. As he said:
The sage Bharata [states]:
"The seed, the drop, the banner, the minor banner, and the purpose."
The five fundamental plot elements are established within the *garbha* juncture.

Thus, their specific nature, if it were to be demonstrated here, would result in excessive prolixity of the text and would be of no use for the present subject; therefore, it has not been stated. || 59 ||
Since no one else whatsoever is capable of acting in this way, therefore:
"Homage to him who makes the non-existent existent, or indeed makes the existent non-existent."
To the one who possesses sovereign power over both the independent and the non-independent, and who alone is the lord of their destruction.

To one who is independent—that is, possessing a power that does not depend on anything else—to effect the non-existence, meaning the dissolution, of existing things (satām) residing in the world; or the existence, meaning their rebirth, of non-existent things (asatām), which, because they have been dissolved, are devoid of manifestation or description; likewise.

To him who— being one and without a second— exults through the gains, losses, and sovereignties (the powers of arising, destruction, and manifestation) of all beings from Brahmā downwards, none of whom are independent, and which [powers] manifest as non-different from himself despite being dependent gains, losses, and sovereignties. || 60 ||
(Page 71) He speaks again in order to praise the Blessed One, whose true nature has been revealed through the excellence of his devotion:
I bow to Him whose single drop (*bindu*) is all the bliss whatsoever that is seen here in the three worlds.
The god, an ocean of bliss. || 61 ||

In this threefold world whose essential nature has been explained, whatever joy— be it of any kind— shines forth from Śiva down to the level of every limited subject, all of that is but a single drop for Him; I bow to that infinite ocean of bliss, the supreme sea of play and other delights.

"I enter [into that]. Thus, even within those various limited joys, the practitioner of yoga (yogijana), whose mind has been made one-pointed, enters into supreme bliss (paramānanda); this is the direction of the instruction shown. As it is said in the venerable Vijñānabhairava:

Through the unfolding of the bliss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the joy produced by eating and drinking, one should contemplate the state of fullness; from that, great bliss (*mahānanda*) shall arise.
Thus, [verse] 61.
Since the Lord is such as this, therefore, oh, Brahmā and the others are truly fortunate!
Those who were liberated from other conversation,
overwhelmed with joy, muttered "Namo namaḥ Śivāya. || 62 ||

Having set aside all other conversation, they became overwhelmed by the joy arising from the power of recitation through one-pointed concentration—that is, they were so agitated by bliss that they forgot all worldly affairs. || 62 ||
Moreover,
[salutations] to the one who ordains infinite desires even for those who are free from desire.
Although the universe is beginningless, salutations be to You, its enjoyer.
Precisely because of being full of bliss, even though she has emerged from desires— that is, from longings—
she [remains] characterized by various enjoyments and liberation.

To the one who accomplishes desired objects; likewise, although beginningless—meaning, although the world has as its primordial and non-dual form that which is eternally manifested from his own screen—he is the enjoyer of the world that has become the object of enjoyment, the one who experiences wonder (camatkartṛ); and how could he, for whom no desires exist, [seek] them?
"He gives," yet he whose nature is "not eating" (an-ādī)—how could such a one be the enjoyer of the universe?
This is the figure of speech known as *virodhālaṃkāra* (the ornament of contradiction). || 63 ||
Moreover, whom shall we praise— the Lord, the primordial nature at the root of the commencement of the three worlds?
Who would lack assistance from him, since his nature is complete? (64)
The three worlds are as previously described; we praise that which is their originating root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*),
the cause of all causes, and therefore the Lord (*īśvara*)— whose power is unimpeded everywhere—
since His nature is absolute sovereignty, a complete attribute that transcends all others.
For one whose very nature is such, who indeed would not desire— that is, would not seek— the benefit consisting in the attainment of sovereignty appropriate to themselves? All [would].
For indeed, Brahmā and the others were created by Maheśvara himself, having been granted mere droplets of their respective powers.
Moreover,
even in the midst of great hardships,
those who are defiled by a flood of delusion—
We praise that Śiva, upon remembering whom all thoughts become serene.
Because they cannot be brought to a conclusion even in great and heavy difficulties—

regarding objects such as the complex purposes of investigating the world and so forth— their cognitions (saṃvids), whose true light is obscured and defiled by the flood of delusion (moha)— that is, by the expansion of Māyā— are [brought to rest] when [He] is remembered.

As soon as He is reflected upon, they become serene—casting off the turbidity of illusion, they become possessed of the knowledge of reality; we praise that Śiva, who consists of supreme bliss, by contemplating Him non-dually. || 65 ||
"All this is easily accomplished by you alone," he said, "O Lord, for it is through you alone that this is possible here."
The power of the Lord is unbreakable;
by His will, the dissolution and emergence of the three worlds are extended.

For him who, by mere will, effects the dissolution and arising of the three worlds, how insignificant is this [power]? But another, however, whose activity depends solely upon you, possesses only fragile power; such is the meaning. || 66 ||
And he says that your sovereignty is so unrestrained that even a wicked deed, when directed toward You,
O Lord, becomes supreme merit.
Even for that which is well-done, there is a further excellence beyond it; therefore, O sir, you are not that [which is merely well-done].

The Lord— the Supreme Lord himself, who is intent on play and other such pastimes— considers even a despicable or forbidden action performed with the thought "I am doing all this" to be a meritorious deed (*sukṛta*), whereas [actions] such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and so forth [are considered otherwise].
Even a well-performed deed (*sukṛta*) is considered a wicked deed (*kukarma*) because the mind is robbed by the desire for its fruit;

therefore, whether one acts with or without the realization of non-difference from the Blessed One (*bhagavad-abheda-bhāvanā*), that alone is the true definition of good and evil deeds. By the words "O, you are That," the unsurpassed [state] is indicated.
One contemplates the supreme nature of the Lord with a state of mind characterized by radiant joy and directed toward the Self. || 67 ||
Since you are such as this, therefore you are seized by the fist; now that you have been seen, where can you go from us?
Thus, the fortunate ones, swelling with the sentiment of devotion, run toward Dhūrjaṭi.
This [Self], shining as pure consciousness throughout all states, has been grasped by the fist—you have been made one’s own;
and this has been seen—you have been directly realized.
You have always remained shining clearly as the very form of the light of consciousness; therefore, for us—our...
Where are you going? Nowhere at all;
you are unable to conceal your true nature, for everything is indeed composed of you alone.

"Shining and established"— those who are "inflated" (adhmātāḥ), that is, whose consciousness is ignited by such a devotional sentiment (bhaktirasa) consisting of constant immersion in You, they "run toward" Dhūrjaṭi— Mahādeva—
following Him with impetuous zeal as He spreads through all states of being.
They contemplate that which is unobstructed by the veil of verbal expression; for this very reason, they are blessed, filled with the supreme treasure, and praiseworthy among the wise. 68.
And what more shall we praise in you, who are the pure essence beyond the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman, and further beyond that?
He whose great, profound, and beautiful ignorance consists of the nature of the Vedas.

We praise You, who are even beyond that which is the supreme *śukra* (semen/vital essence) of the three Vedas beginning with the *Ṛgveda*— which consists of the non-dual awareness (*abhedavimarśamaya*) and takes the form of the light of the *praṇava*, whose nature is the manifestation of the sun of consciousness; for Yours is this command (*ājñā*), the injunction consisting of the Vedas themselves.
The knowledge of the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the statements belonging to the *karmakāṇḍa*, the *devatākāṇḍa*, and the *jñānakāṇḍa* is possessed by only a few.

She is "profound" because she is attainable; she is "beautiful" because, according to the perspective taught in the Vedāntas—that Brahman is consciousness and bliss—she bestows repose in supreme bliss.
And the intention of one who speaks thus is this: that the meaning of the Veda consists of this very nature of command.

It is established that [the word] exists when there is an authorizer (*niyoktṛ*)—one who commands; otherwise, how could an insentient word possess the capacity for syntactic connection or the status of being an authorizer? And although the Lord’s status as an authorizer has indeed been stated by the Gāyatrī itself, it is not perceived by the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) due to their insentience. As he will state:
"By the Gāyatrī is sung that which impels the splendor of the intellects.
Thus [ends verse 69].
Having thus praised the instigator (niyoktṛ) who is obtained through the investigation of injunctions (niyoga) in the form of commands,
he states that even the position of the meaning of prescriptive sentences (vidhi-vākya-artha) possesses a Lord:
"You are the beginning as well as the end of the injunction."
O Supreme Lord of the universe, how could that multitude of dharma which has proceeded from you not exist? 70.

The injunction (*vidhi*) consisting of forms such as "one should sacrifice" and "one should not kill" is the differentiation between what is to be done and its opposite; therein, the "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to the enjoiner (*vidhātṛ*), and the "end" (*anta*) refers to the manifestation of the respective fruits through the accomplishment of the enjoined matter.

The meaning is that you alone are everything—the independent conscious self—and thus you manifest in the form of injunctions and so forth. Otherwise, if the entire collection of attributes of the universe—that is, the diverse activity of its inherent nature—had not proceeded from you, how could it come to be? Without you, it simply would not exist.
The meaning is that nothing whatsoever can manifest without the wall of light [as its substratum]. As those who know the Upanishads have said:
"Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined."
Thus, by the very [discussion of] injunction, the position that the productive urge (bhāvanā) is the object has also been answered. || 70 ||
If everything is composed of the Blessed One according to the Upanishads (Śrutyanta),

then why is knowledge alone not taught in the ritual sections (Karmakāṇḍa), and how is that very same thing prohibited in the sections on knowledge (Jñānakāṇḍa)? He dispels this doubt by means of praise.
Salutations to you who, having manifested the delusion of those bewildered by worldly existence, shatters that very delusion.
And having chosen the bliss of knowledge, which is free from dualities, O Lord, they reveal it. || 71 ||
O Lord, those who are deluded in this world— within the cycle of existence (saṃsāra)—

due to the power of Your illusory energy (māyā-śakti), and who, because of that very delusion, are attached to duality and devoted to ritual action (karman), [you remove] for them, in the initial stage, each respective error of duality.
Having manifested it within the sphere of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), he breaks through [the veil] for the sake of destruction;
likewise, having chosen the knowledge-bliss— the consciousness that is the supreme non-dual form— which is composed of bliss,
he first conceals it from the unqualified because of its secret nature, and subsequently [reveals it] to the qualified.

Salutations to You who reveal—that is, clarify—[the truth]. And thus, that very nature of the *karmakāṇḍa* which was shown by the Blessed One as something to be abandoned (*heyatvena*) because it constitutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), is instead accepted as something to be adopted (*upādeyatvena*) by the deluded, and the status of the *jñānakāṇḍa* as mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is asserted. Now...

Or rather, by the Blessed One himself, for the sake of protecting the fourfold duties such as creation, those who possess such confidence were deluded and established [in that state]. "Saṃbhrāntim" is a corrupt reading. || 71 ||
Just as the Supreme Lord, having manifested and then dispelled delusion within various scriptures such as the Vedic Saṃhitās,
reveals the bliss of knowledge, so too may He shatter the illusion manifested before us and illuminate that very bliss of knowledge; thus he says.
By what desires could the limit of this illusion be reached, which is traversed in the blink of an eye?
May Śiva protect us, stealing that [darkness] away. || 72 ||

By which knowers, beginning with Brahmā, or by which mental longings could that particular excellence— the ultimate limit of Māyā, whose nature is the non-manifestation of the non-difference from Consciousness— characterized by the attainment of the state of non-dual Consciousness,
be reached? For this [excellence] is beyond even all mental longings.
Śiva— the bestower of ultimate bliss— steals away that illusion in a single moment, removing it by the mere unfolding of his own true nature; [he does this] for us.
May she protect—may she guard me—from the sphere of illusory mental impressions, so that even by name, non-apprehension (akhyāti) may no longer remain. || 72 ||
He reveals the profound course of dispassion— that specific excellence reaching the limit of illusion which is visible only to those possessed of devotion.
O Lord, you are the master of those who bear the supreme glory of knowledge and the highest pinnacle of desirelessness. 73.
O Lord, O Supreme God, [he attained] the state of detachment— meaning freedom from craving for sense objects—
which has reached its highest limit and regards even the station of Sadāśiva and other such levels as mere straw;
as well as the supreme realization of knowledge, that is, the awakening to reality, according to the Vaiṣṇava and Lākula traditions.

By abandoning the limited knowledge taught in the Pāśupata and other such systems, one attains Śrī— the supreme manifestation— which consists of the self-revelation of the supreme non-dual Self, which is transcendent of the universe yet identical with the universe, beautiful with the bliss of consciousness, autonomous, and eternally luminous; that is, the supreme sovereignty.
Likewise, regarding dispassion (*naiḥspṛhya*)— that is,
turning away from the search for the means to attain the glory of the aforementioned knowledge— and [attaining] the supreme—
When someone has said that the peak of realization has been ascended— which consists in the casting aside of all mudrās, mantras, meditations, and the like—
while the reality of existence stands manifest in its entirety before one's eyes;
Those by whom means are elaborated surely do not know you.

Thus, those who bear—carry—such a supreme pinnacle of repose in desirelessness, they who have seen beyond the veil of *māyā*, are your subjects; you are their Lord, and they are your unimpeded servants. Therefore, for people such as us, you [remove] *māyā* by a mere glance.
The meaning is that you rob [them]. || 73 ||
And you are their uncommon lord; thus he said:
"You are the Brahman even of Brahmā; you are the master of whom, O Ruler?"
Who indeed can know how much you are, the auspiciousness of the auspiciousness of the world?
In the midst of the world— the universe— that which is auspicious— namely Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva—
even for them, that which is auspicious is the benefactor through the manifestation of one's own self as a mass of perfect consciousness and bliss.
"Who knows how great is your majesty?"— the meaning is that your greatness is immeasurable—
because you are superior even to Brahmā, who is the form of the Great Light and the object of meditation for the Vedāntins,
since you possess the power of Brahman’s sovereignty by bestowing upon him the power to create the universe.
And it is nourishing. As it is said in the Gītā:
"My womb is the Great Brahman; in that I place the seed.
From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings occurs."
Thus [it is said]:
"O Lord, how much fruit could this neuter supreme Brahman bear,
were it not for Your beautiful Śakti who impels its manly power?"
Thus, you are not merely the lord of some [deity] from Brahmā down to Śiva; rather, you are the master of everything. 74.
And for this reason, what is the use of other kinsmen? And furthermore—
O Lord, you are my friend and likewise my master in every situation; you are the one who delivers me from the ocean of worldly existence. 75.

O Lord—whose nature is to prevail everywhere—you perform for me all that ought to be done for my benefit in every situation—that is, in every occasion involving friends and other kinsmen—since you accomplish even for the world that which is impossible: the rescue from the ocean of existence, which is so difficult to cross; therefore...
What is the use of others, such as kinsmen and the like? || 75 ||
Thus, reeling from the savoring of the supreme nectar awakened by the weight of intense devotion, he said:
"Victorious are those [teachings] capable of washing away the impurities of delusion, illusion, and the like!"
Drops of divine nectar were drawn forth by the power of Śiva-yoga.

Delusion—namely non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), which is the *āṇava* impurity; Māyā, which is the *māyīya* impurity; and by the word "etcetera," the *kārma* impurity as well; [these are] capable of thoroughly washing away—that is, eradicating—these impurities.

By the power of Śaiva yoga—that is, through the excellence of absorption into Māheśvara—the divine drops of nectar (divyapīyūṣavipruṣaḥ), which are particles of supreme bliss, have been drawn forth; they are brought forth by sheer force from the belly of Māyā, and they triumph—they exist with preeminence over all. || 76 ||
Even so, expressing the aspiration that "may the Supreme Lord cause my intellects to remain ever-striving for immersion alone even during the occasions of emergence," he says:
"He whose [glory] is sung by the Gāyatrī..."
May that Lord, the impeller of the splendor of our intellects, also inspire our thoughts toward the path of the righteous. 77.

In this auspicious inquiry, the venerable light— the supreme splendor— belonging to that Great Lord, the Sun of Awakening, [is revealed] through the Gāyatrī, which is the embodiment of the power of speech.

The "measure of the Vedas" (vedamātrā)— that which impels all cognitions belonging to every subject and grasps the determination of their respective duties— is praised; that Lord, who is capable of manifesting everywhere,
[is he] perhaps our own cognitions surfacing during the intervals of worldly activity?

One should impel all the functions of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*) toward the true path, which is the nature of immersion, the means for attaining the Supreme Lord—meaning one should cause them to exert effort by setting aside all other activities. And the intention of the phrase "on the true path" is this:
that which has been thus set forth by the *Gāyatrī* itself regarding the Blessed One...

Even by those foolish Vedic scholars who recite it day after day and yet do not understand it, its nature as the impeller of all-cognizing wisdom is not perceived; thus, this exhortation toward the wrong path is indeed the work of those very people. || 77 ||
Alternatively, enough with the request for immersion; or rather, even by means of a prayer that makes my mind one-pointed upon the forms of earth and the other elements as non-different from myself—
for you, indeed, are gracious to me in the states of immersion.
Once you have become purified through the subsiding of the turbidity of illusion, you will perform all those [deeds] within all the forms beginning with earth.
He says this [to show] that his own nature, which consists of everything, will manifest without delay:
"O you of eight forms, do you not abide even in a single form among us?"
Or, being pleased, you shall make everything eternal; indeed, you will accomplish all things.

The intended meaning of the term "eightfold form" (*aṣṭamūrti*) is that the Blessed One alone exists through these forms, beginning with Earth and ending with the Sacrificer (*yajamāna*), such that even the name of duality does not exist. Furthermore, this supposition is appropriate in the sense of a future action, as expressed by the word "you will do" (*kariṣyasi*), because:
The true nature of things generally consists in their capacity for causal efficiency; yet for you, O Lord, even your name alone possesses this power.
It bestows the accomplishment culminating in liberation. || 79 ||

He is the Lord (*īśa*) of all categories of entities— consisting of the principles (*tattva*), the worlds (*bhuvana*), and their presiding deities— which, for the most part, exist as objective realities according to worldly convention, capable of performing their respective specific causal functions (*arthakriyā*).

Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), according to the established view in this context that "even the name of Dhūrjaṭi grants great accomplishment culminating in liberation to those who meditate upon it," the "dough-sticks" (*daṇḍairapūpāḥ*) have been explained. By the use of the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*), this is stated in accordance with worldly convention.
For from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is implied that the true nature of all things is their being identical with the Blessed One.
Who indeed does not acknowledge your supramundane majesty? Thus he says:
"The ever-renewing wonder of the world... [79]
O Lord, what wise person would not be filled with wonder by that power of yours which is able to conceive of various other states of existence? (80)
O Lord, that which goes through each and every state, from the immobile beings up to the divine wombs,

and assumes the forms of those various [beings] such as Brahmā and others, is the world— the multitude of living beings; that very thing is the "wondrous" (citra) of that innumerable [multitude], at every moment.

To infer— that is, to reason out and determine— the various states of existence, which consist of the manifold diversity of the continuum of consciousness, each with its own infinite branches: this is possible for you, the omniscient one, and not for anyone else.

*Śakti* means capacity; by that [capacity], one who is endowed with an excellent mind consisting of the contemplation of identity with You is a wise person (*manasvin*). Who indeed would not be struck with wonder?

Everyone is indeed filled with wonder, as the internal throbbing [of realization] is manifested through the *sāttvika* emotions such as horripilation, which are marked by the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of astonishment.
It consists of supreme bliss alone. || 80 ||
Furthermore,
what is difficult to do he makes easy to do,
and likewise, he turns suffering into happiness.
We remember him who has mindfulness as his sole hero, the enemy of the battle [of the senses]. 81.

We remember— that is, we contemplate through non-differentiation— that enemy of Smara (Śiva), who effects an extraordinary manifestation; for even the mere remembrance of Him makes easy that which is difficult for anyone else to perform, namely, the immersion into the power of Rudra, because it cannot be accomplished by another.
to accomplish [it] with mere ease; likewise, suffering— the repository of all suffering— [is to be abandoned].
To bring joy to the delusion of Māyā—that is, to transform it into that which consists of supreme bliss—the Ekavīrā is she whose power is independent of anything else and who is unimpeded. || 81 ||
And because the Blessed One possesses such unsurpassed power, for this very reason he said:
"Victorious are those songs of which He, the Supreme Lord, is the subject."
By whose very name great-souled ones are made to bristle with horripilation.

"Great" (mahān) refers to those whose self has been made to blossom by the power of immersion (*samāveśa*) arising through the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*); according to the aforementioned principle, even by their name reaching the path of hearing during the state of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*), they are covered with sprouts of horripilation and are once again immersed [in that state]. That [state] belongs to them.
Let other matters rest for now; even the songs devoted to His contemplation—even the hymns of praise—triumph, existing in a state of supreme excellence. || 82 ||

"There is nothing whatsoever that can serve as a comparison for you," he said by means of the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-comparison): "O Bhava, only if you yourself were like yourself could there be a comparison."
The creation and withdrawal of the three worlds are manifested through the array of his own powers. || 83 ||

"Bhava" is as before; you alone are the Supreme, by whom the creation and withdrawal of the aforementioned three worlds are accomplished—that is, brought forth—by the "array" (vyūha) of your own powers such as Will and the rest, which consists in manifesting their various states of being as either subordinate or predominant qualities. If indeed you are that...
The meaning is that it is exclusively unique. || 83 ||
Therefore,
you are the mantra, you are the one to be consulted, and you are the counselor; other than you, how could there be another?
"O Lord, grant that mantra to me, so that I may become one with your mantra. (84)

O Lord, whatever mantra there may be— whether consisting of four *kalās*, nine *ātmas*, and so forth— which possesses the nature of reflecting (*manana*) and protecting (*trāṇa*), whose ultimate reality is the perfect self-reflection of "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃvimarśa*), that is You alone; and those who recite it (*tanmantriṇaḥ*) are likewise You.

You alone are the great light-natured self; you alone are the one who recites this mantra, the object of recitation, and the reciter—the one who reflects—since there exists nothing else whatsoever apart from consciousness. Therefore, being such as you are, [bestow] that mantra, which consists of the forms of the mantra, the object of the mantra, and the reciter, upon me.
Therefore, grant [this], so that I may become exactly like you— whose mantra consists of the aforementioned triad—

such that the distinction between the mantra, the object of the mantra (*mantrya*), and the one who recites the mantra (*mantrayitṛ*) has dissolved, and I may exist as nothing but you alone. And it is said in the *Śrīkaṇṭhasaṃhitā*:
The mantra is separate and the practitioner is separate; [if they are so conceived,] one never attains success.
All this has its root in knowledge; without knowing it, one certainly does not succeed.
Thus [ends verse] 84.
And because this [universe] has arisen from Him, he says:
"You are the Self whose nature is light and whose will is true; I too am He."
Is this transmigratory existence the Lord himself?
Even that dream—how could it exist in you? (85)
(94) He— my own self— whose nature is light, who is a mass of radiance, whose will is true, and whose essence consists of the ontological self-reflection of the perfect "I," he too am I.
"Am I not of such a vast form, a transmigrating being— abiding in the state of saṃsāra— or rather,
is it you yourself who clearly manifest as this 'I'? For in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*),
when one is flooded with the impressions of the essence of samādhi, there is but a slight [manifestation] due to the predominance of the body and so forth to a mere degree."

Does that which flashes forth as if it were transmigratory existence constitute a dream? For a dream can only be conceived as a mere appearance when there is an absence of the manifest state of being a subject consisting of the body and so forth; and that [dreaming] is not possible for You, whose nature is pure consciousness alone. Since You Yourself are my Self, consisting of the expansion of the Fourth State (turya) that transcends even the Fourth (turyātīta), to whom would it belong?

Let the dream appear; yet, since there is no one whatsoever who serves as the substratum for its appearance, there is in no way even a flicker of transmigratory existence through delusion—thus, I am eternally Śiva alone. || 85 ||
And since you alone exist as me, manifesting in every way,
and there is no other so-called "I" who performs any action or experiences anything, therefore, in this manner—

By means of the general statement that for those who have pacified their sense of selfhood (*ahaṃbhāva*) and renounced all actions along with their fruits, that sovereignty which consists solely of being absorbed in You is the one thing worthy of praise, he says: "That is refined;
that is not vulgar."
That alone is logical:
that sovereignty which was bestowed upon you, O Lord, by the surrender of the fruits of action.

It is indestructible (*abhaṅgi*), imperishable (*anaśvaram*), and indivisible (*avibhāgam*). That which arises within a collection of villages, senses, objects, and individual knowers is "vulgar" (*grāmyam*); because it possesses fluctuation between excellence and deficiency, it is contemptible.
That which is not such is "non-vulgar" (*agrāmyam*)—the most excellent of all—and for this very reason, it is "logical" (*upapattimat*), since it does not depend on the perspective of another.
For the sake of truth. || 86 ||
Thus, overflowing with such reflection on the reality of things, praising his very own self, he says:
(page 96)
Who is capable of destroying what misfortune,
or of not bestowing what prosperity?
He who is such is our beloved.
The god of gods, whose banner bears the bull.
"The Bull (vṛṣa) is Dharma; it is indeed a quality of the Lord, consisting of perception and action.
Because He sustains both the conscious and the unconscious, He is called 'Dharma' by the wise.
According to this principle stated by the venerable [author], the Bull is Dharma—whose nature is the equilibrium of knowledge and action—and the Banner (dhvaja)—
He who possesses such characteristics is our beloved—our dear one. To explain what kind he is, [the author] says:
he who is capable of destroying every single misfortune whatsoever, and indeed capable of bestowing every single prosperity whatsoever. || 87 ||
And for this reason, he says that devotion alone toward You, who are thus omnipotent, is the cause for attaining one's desired goal,
for one who is blinded by the impurity consisting of *māyā*:
O Lord, devotion to you is the supreme collyrium for purifying the divine eye of wisdom. 88.
Illusion itself is the disease— the affliction— and the impurity produced by it is the obscuration.
For one who is blind by that— whose light is obscured— the divine eye of supramundane gnosis [is obstructed].
For one who seeks the attainment of full manifestation, devotion to You alone is the supreme ointment for the purpose of purification—that is, regarding the unfolding of one's true nature. || 88 ||
And therefore, that which is fearless, which consists of bliss (ānandamaya), which is one, and which is imperishable— [that is Brahman].
"O God, grant me your foot;
come quickly! Why do you wait? (89)

O Deva, come— submerging the concealment of your own nature, appear before me; and then [behold] that which consists of bliss, non-dual, imperishable, and fearless— that in the presence of which the fear of saṃsāra ceases to exist,
and regarding which even the fear of the suspicion of retreat does not arise— such as this is that which...
The "place"— the abode of rest— grant that to me quickly; swiftly place me within your own self.
"Enter! Why do you wait? Do not delay even for a single moment!"—this is the speech of one intensely longing and overflowing with love. (89)
Again, overflowing with the weight of devotion, he said:
"Aha! This ocean of saṃsāra is naturally profound and terrible!"
Oh! Maheśvara is truly some supreme means for crossing over that [ocean of existence]. || 90 ||

It is naturally profound because it is difficult to cross even for Brahmā and the other gods; it is "terrible" (*ghora*) because it consists of suffering, and for that very reason, it is like an ocean. It is "somehow" (*ko'pi*) attainable only by those possessed of devotion; it is the peerless, supreme means whose ultimate reality is consciousness alone, and thus it brings one effortlessly and instantaneously to the further shore. Two.
The two words "aho" express extreme wonder. || 90 ||
Even when considering his various modes of manifestation, he says the following to praise the Blessed One for possessing qualities that are both unique and unsurpassed:
"Homage to him who has brought an end to the end-maker (Kṛtakṛtānta)."
To you, the crusher of Mada;
to him upon whose head the Gaṅgā is placed; to the one who accomplishes what is appropriate. || 91 ||
It was appropriate to subdue Time and Desire, who were intoxicated by causing universal calamity;

yet it was even more appropriate to show favor by bearing Gaṅgā upon one’s own head— she who, being purifying and beneficial to the world, consists of the flow of tears of joy born from one's own eyes at the touch of the Goddess's hand.
The performance of the purpose as it has been joined [to it]. || 91 ||
Since you alone are transcendent over the universe even while possessing such a form, therefore you alone are the refuge for those who desire fruits that transcend the universe; thus he says:
*aiśvaryajñānavairāgya-*... [and so forth].
O Protector, for those who seek a state even above all phenomena (dharmas), what other refuge is there besides you? (92)

(So page 100) Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the expansion resulting from the existence of objects to be ruled over; knowledge (*jñāna*) is the ascertainment of things to be abandoned and things to be acquired; dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the absence of craving for sense-objects; and virtue (*dharma*)—

The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) bestowed by the activity that brings about the excellence of the qualities of being— [a process] which has established its footing even in those beginning with Brahmā— belongs to those who pray for a higher station in the pure conscious Self;
You alone are their goal and refuge, and no other, because others are veiled by the fourfold [powers] such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
Indeed, such unsurpassed sovereignty belongs to you alone; for,
O Śambhu, when you do not will it, who is capable of bending even a blade of grass?
But who, favored by your will, would not bear the yoke of Brahma? (93)

Let alone the acts of creation and so forth; without Your will, not even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or others are capable of bending even a blade of grass. Yet, by the grace of Your power, who could not bear the office of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the rest? Even a mere insect would be capable of bearing it.
As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*: "The power of Brahmā belongs to the Supreme One alone; wherever there is His will, there He should cause [it] to fall."
Thus it is said; likewise, Viṣṇu is remembered [as the deity] of the Vaiṣṇavī [mudrā]. || 93 ||
And therefore,
those whose heads are crowned with the intense brilliance of the ruby-like diadem of Śiva’s prostration;
To whom would those whose wealth is wisdom pay homage, or whom would they cause to bow down? || 94 ||
For Hara—the Great Lord—prostration itself is a ruby crown;

a crown made of jewels that manifests his sovereignty. With such [a crown], their heads are exalted—that is, their heads are raised high—those who are rich in wisdom, whose wealth is the realization of reality. Who [else]...?

They do not bow down to anyone, even to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the rest; moreover, this statement is far too limited—for whom among those such as Brahmā would they not cause to bow? They would cause everyone indeed to prostrate before them.
Desiring that very immersion which constitutes the greatness of this prostration, he says:
"The unshakable lake of nectar, free from all delusion."
O Dhūrjaṭi, even though you sit in the very midst of the ocean of the knowledge of existence, [you remain untouched]. 95.

O Dhūrjaṭi— O Mahādeva— when shall I dwell within the nectar-lake, which is the essence of the ocean of your knowledge— that ocean of your own radiance— and which consists of the nature of the power of blissful autonomy?

May we attain identification with that— what kind of lake of nectar is it? It is that which is unwavering, having been attained through the firm rooting out of all delusions— that is, the abandonment of all ignorances— and which consists of the very sovereignty of the Lord, whose nature is light, and whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), becoming the very heart of one's being.
As the venerable author of the *Pratyabhijñā* has said:
"Consciousness, whose essence is self-reflective awareness, is the supreme speech (*parāvāk*) arising from its own inherent nature;
this is the primary sovereignty, the supreme lordship of the Self."
Thus [ends the verse] 95.
He says that even a mere form of Yours, when encountered in a painting or through mental construction, produces what kind of prosperity for devotees—
wonderful indeed, that even when seen in a picture...
Or even when it has merely entered the realm of aspiration,
O Protector, you bestow the perfectly complete fruit of the ultimate truth.

No one indeed performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*) by means of an unreal form, such as that delineated by a mental construction of a painting; however, how could the Supreme Lord—who is the presence of all things—not fully engender the blossoming of supreme bliss for his devotees through whatever form? Thus it is here.
In the verse beginning with "Homage even to those who abide in manifold conceptualizations," [the Lord] is shown as existing within dreams;

in the passage beginning with "to him whose desires have been withdrawn," he is shown as established in the external world; in places such as "O Lord, what are you not? he is shown as consisting of the universe; and in statements such as "that which is not divided even when things are divided," he is shown as undivided.

The nature of the Blessed One is a mass of consciousness and bliss; for this person, who is entirely composed of the Blessed One through devotion that has reached its ultimate limit, [this nature] exists in every respect.
It indeed bestows the fruit of the action. || 96 ||
Thus, who is superior to you in virtues?
And who is more devoid of virtues than you?
Thus, O Lord, do we praise you? Or do we revile you? We do not know. (97)

Regarding the phrase "superior to you in qualities"—meaning in omniscience and so forth—it has been stated that no one is superior to you; indeed, even an equal does not exist for you, as expressed by the saying, "If there were anyone like you, they would be you alone. How then could there be anyone superior? Furthermore, who else besides you could be superior while being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), given that [others] are conditioned by the impressions of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest?
The meaning is that there is no other whatsoever who is untouched [by you]. By these two statements, we do not know the truth as to whether they result in censure or praise regarding you;
for even that censure directed toward those possessing qualities such as *sattva* and the like—which possess no superior qualities—is, because the universe consists of you, directed toward you alone.
Or rather,
is praise— which consists either of [pointing out] a deficiency in qualities or of [asserting] a preponderance of qualities— ultimately established in you, the Self of the Universe?

Thus, reflecting upon this twofold statement regarding You who consist of the Great Non-duality, we have ascended the swing of doubt. For in reality, since Your form is indivisible, there is neither praise nor blame; such is the ultimate truth. 97.
Therefore, enough for now with this deliberation on these two statements;
even in the mere chanting [of it], the fruit of your grace is a flood of nectar.
O Lord of the World, who else is capable even of drinking it, much less of giving it? (98)

O Lord of the Universe, by the grace of Your favor— which consists of the manifestation of Your own purity— may one drink that fruit, full of wonder, which arises even from the mere utterance of Your name, You who are the flood of nectar in the form of supreme bliss.
Because it is inward-turned and without rest, not even anyone beginning with Brahmā is capable of even savoring it,
let alone giving or bestowing it; you alone are able to give that.
This is the meaning. || 98 ||
Therefore, with the desire to obtain the supreme accomplishment from such a master, he speaks in order to pray for devotion alone: "The object of all that is to be prayed for..."
O Lord, because you are the treasury that fulfills all goals, I pray to you in every way only to obtain devotion unto you. 99.

O Lord, since you, the Supreme Sovereign, are the treasury from which all desired objects are produced, I pray to you for devotion to you alone in every way, and not for any fruit whatsoever. || 99 ||
He demonstrates that devotion culminates in supreme accomplishment by way of a salutation to the Blessed One: "Homage to the Lord of the Three Worlds."
Salutations to you, O Bhava,
who possess the power to remove obstacles for those devoted to you, by granting the lordship over the three worlds.

(107) Salutations to You, the Lord of the Three Worlds— the Sovereign of the Universe— who, for those who resort to You— those possessed of devotion to You— bestow the previously determined status of being the Lord of the three worlds.
In the manifestation of the identity of one's own self with Viśveśvara, he possesses the power of Vināyaka— that is, unimpeded sovereignty.
Therefore,
[he is the cause] of the complete destruction of all afflictions.
When doubt arises as to who the cause is, one resolves, "O Lord, it is you"; who, having so determined, has not gone to you for refuge? (101)

O Supreme Lord, having doubted what might be the cause for the pacification of all afflictions such as ignorance, and having resolved that "You are He" and "You alone are such," who would not take refuge in You? All those possessed of discernment worship You, the destroyer of all afflictions; thus, devotion to You alone [is the means].
It is the cause for the pacification of all afflictions, just as it is for the attainment of lordship over the three worlds. || 101 ||
Therefore,
having enjoyed worldly pleasures, [one experiences] the wandering in existence...
"Having abandoned [this world], I shall attain the supreme state"—
such an aspiration here would be fitting for one who possesses supreme devotion to Śambhu. (102)

In Śambhu—the mass of consciousness and bliss—this aspiration may shine only for some rare devotee. Asking "What is this?", he says: "Having abandoned the delusion of worldly existence"—that is, having discarded non-recognition (*akhyāti*) in its entirety—and [enjoying] the pleasures that have arrived, drawn by the power of yoga.

"Having eaten, I shall attain the supreme state"— thinking thus, one should not harbor attachment or pride when invited by those established in the Maheśvara doctrine which consists of supreme non-duality, because that would lead again to undesirable consequences (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 3.51).
Thus, according to the principles of other scriptures, attachment to enjoyments never leads to bondage for one who has realized the true nature of reality. As it is said in the *Śrī Spanda*:
Therefore, in the contemplations of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva; he alone, as the enjoyer, is eternally established everywhere in the form of the object of enjoyment.
(3.2.2) Thus [ends the section]. || 202 ||
Therefore,
O Protector, whatever I might do or say, whether good or bad, even in a dream—
"Because of the pride of being dependent on you, I am everywhere here at ease. (103)

O Lord, whatever I might do with my mind or body, or speak with my voice— even in a dream consisting of delusion— whether it be in accordance with the scriptures or otherwise, in all such cases I am at ease, being composed solely of Your bliss; for what pride can there be in [anything other than] dependence on You?

"I am indeed you, the Great Lord, the conscious self; in all states, I perform all this"—with such an enthusiasm rooted in dependence on you, [there arises] that which consists of the firm support of non-difference from you.
(Page 110)
The meaning is: "I have no suffering whatsoever, anywhere, at any time. || 103 ||
He says that there is not even a touch of ignorance for me: "In that abode of yours, which is the light even of lights, I run."
I consider this touch of darkness by the mind to be like the younger brother of the son of a barren woman. || 104 ||
O Lord, independent one! Even for the luminaries—such as the sun, moon, fire, and so forth—which are themselves objects of knowledge, You are the light, the illuminator;
in that abode of Yours, the radiance of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), there is no contact with darkness for the mind as it rushes toward You, flowing without any interval.
I consider "attachment through ignorance" to be like the younger brother of the son of a barren woman; here, the meaning of the sentence functions as the object.
By stating, "The son of a barren woman does not even exist, so how could he have a younger brother—a younger sibling?"—he demonstrates that my non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is absolutely non-existent.
And it is a fitting statement that even the name of darkness does not exist on the ground of supreme light. 104.
Or rather, let alone following after Your manifestation; I believe that even my zeal for devotion to You produces the fruit of boons— thus he says,
"he too has set his foot [upon that path]."
For one whose desire is fixed upon the secure path to liberation,
thinking "I shall serve Śiva," this [path] is established. 105.

"Śiva" means consisting of the supreme good (*śreyas*); "I shall serve" means I shall take refuge [in Him] by becoming one with Him. Thus, for me, whose resolve consists of such extraordinary enthusiasm, I am [the one] on the path to liberation—that is, to *apavarga*, which consists in attaining non-difference from Śiva—on the secure path, namely, in the abode of Śakti (*śākta-dhāman*).

For the sake of security, supreme excellence, and welfare, he has placed his feet—upon which the powers of his own innate knowledge and action have been established; thus, for him, enthusiasm directed toward devotion alone becomes the bestower of desired goals.
(Page 112)
As was said by our venerable masters:
"Arise! I shall praise Śaṅkara; I shall worship Maheśvara"—only the fortunate ones enjoy such an outburst of passionate devotion.
And so forth. || 105 ||
With the intention that "Śiva is eternally manifest as the benefactor of the universe by his very nature," and thus our desired goal is indeed accomplished, he says:
"By means of the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the world..."
In this world, regarding the functions of the triad,
O Lord, Your power alone perceives the independent tantra.

Sustenance (*sthiti*) is attachment to various enjoyments; origination (*utpatti*) is the generation of appropriate bodies, worlds, and so forth for those who have been deluded by dissolution; and dissolution (*laya*) is for the sake of granting rest for a certain period to those exhausted by their continuous succession of enjoyments.
The withdrawal [of the universe] by them for the benefit of the world; here, in this world, O Lord— O Master—
Your power alone is non-dual, and the *tantra* is independent, that is, dependent upon Yourself.
He perceives the *tantraṇa*, which is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). And it is said in the *Mṛgendrāgama*:
"Even while in sleep, he remains awakening those capable of being awakened, obstructing those who are to be obstructed, and accomplishing the actions of those engaged in ritual action."
Making the powers of illusion (māyā-śakti) manifestable, one should perceive everything— the entire collection of things— exactly as it is.
Thus [ends the verse]. 106.
And just as you demonstrate the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe by mere will, so too do you alone bestow grace upon those worthy of it; thus he says:
"Who here in the three worlds is the protector?"
Even when tormented by women, you were not afflicted;
homage be to you, who are that lake of the nectar of nirvāṇa.
He is the Protector (*trātaḥ*), the pacifier of the fear of *saṃsāra*; here, in this world,
by whom [is one protected] from the threefold affliction (*tritāpa*) consisting of the internal, the celestial, and the elemental?
No one is merely scorched; everyone is utterly tormented. It is proclaimed from the highest Brahman down to the smallest insect that no one is truly happy.
Everyone who desires to live undergoes various such transformations.

Thus: *ataḥ*—therefore, *te*—to you alone, to that certain *asāmānya* (uncommon) one, *namaḥ*; you who are the *amṛtahradaḥ*—the ocean of the bliss of supreme non-duality—for the *nirvāṇe*—the quenching—of that *viśvopatāpa*—universal affliction. || 107 ||
With the intention that "the greatness of devotion to you is boundless, and therefore our prayer for it is entirely appropriate," he says:
"Even artificial devotion to you..."
"If this [action] were free from deceit and resulted in an uncontrived fruit, tell me, what would its fruit be? (108)
Even that devotion toward you, the Great God, which is artificial— though it may be accomplished through external worship, meditation, recitation of mantras, and so forth— is also [devotion].

In that state which consists of the arising of the fruit whose nature is the attainment of the uncreated, if the life-force (*asu*) there were free from artifice—sincere, independent of external means, and surging with great passion—then what would its fruit be? With what fruit would it be endowed? Let this be told by you, for it consists of immersion into You, who are the very self of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
The meaning is that no fruit whatsoever can be conceived as superior to devotion to you. || 108 ||
Therefore, you are seen by that eye which belongs to those endowed with devotion;
you are reached by that path by which they go.
O Unborn One, that fruit has been produced from the wish-fulfilling tree of Your discourse.

That unborn one is that eye—that very illuminating knowledge by which you are seen, that is, directly realized; for any other knowledge is indeed non-knowledge. Because it possesses the attribute of illumination, "eye" here refers to knowledge; that is the goal.
That is right practice, by which— consisting of worship, recitation, and meditation,
and accomplished through body, speech, and mind— you are reached; any other, however, leads one into the pit of saṃsāra.
It is indeed a state of no-way-out; thus, that alone is the perfect fruit, obtainable through the performance of actions preceded by knowledge—
which is born from Your discourse, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree because it bestows all prosperity, and which consists of the expansion of supreme bliss— whereas anything else is...
Since every fruit is to be abandoned, it is indeed fruitless. || 109 ||
And therefore,
this state of yours hereafter, which is established in you, is indeed the better for the sake of the highest good.
Therefore, O Lord, you are my refuge for the removal of those obstacles. || 110 ||

Of all the forms of ultimate welfare— consisting of the attainment of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva— this alone is the highest excellence, this alone is the true welfare: which is this state of abiding within You, who are a mass of consciousness and bliss.

...rest; and therefore, for the sake of removing— that is, for the destruction of— those obstacles to that supreme good which arise from within the very midst [of existence] through contact with the non-recognition (*akhyāti*) of You, O [Lord].

O Lord, O Master, you alone are my refuge; act in such a way that at no time, even during the state of emergence (vyutthāna), may non-recognition (akhyāti) ever touch me—this is the meaning. || 110 ||
Thus, reeling from the essence of ecstatic immersion (*samāveśa*) surging forth from contemplating the true nature of the Blessed One, he said with wonder:
"Oh, how most delicious is Śarva— !"
The nectar-essence of the hope for service—
wherein, even in a mere fraction of time, it does not grow ever new? (111)
This very aspiration—the prayer "May I serve Śiva"—which arises from service to Śarva, that is, devotion to Mahādeva, is nectar; its essence is its wondrous charm. Oh, how marvelous!
It is most delicious, being supremely desirable even for a single moment.
It is impossible to abandon that which, at any place—
even for a mere fraction (*kalā*) or portion (*aṃśa*) of time— does not become ever-new; rather, it consists of ever-new wonder at every moment.
Thus, unlike other flavors, it does not bring about a loss of relish through incessant tasting. || 111 ||
Since the greatness of the desire for service to him is such,
he— resting not for a moment— [creates] the three worlds through hundreds of mental constructions.
Even while conceptualizing, he alone remains free from conceptualization; the unborn one is victorious. || 112 ||

Thus, even within worldly transaction, the Lord, entering into the body and so forth, remains indeed unceasing— never resting— in the process of joining and separating the various appearances of subjects and objects at every moment.
One may, by will, manifest externally that very mass of objects which is already shining within.
Thus, according to the established meaning as determined in the *Pratyabhijñākārikā*,
[the reality] resides within all levels of subjects— beginning with Rudra and the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*)— and consists of existence, non-existence, and that which transcends existence.

Victorious is that Unborn One, the most excellent of all, who, though constantly manifesting the triple world through hundreds of conceptualizations— that is, through thousands of modalities— by means of the manifold variety of his fivefold activities, remains solely the supreme reality of stainless, autonomous, luminous consciousness.
It proceeds, yet how can it be non-conceptual when joined with hundreds of conceptual constructions? This is a marvel! He is someone unique, without equal. || 112 ||
He utters a prayer appropriate for praise: "By [thee], who burns the wick of the latent tendencies of saṃsāra smeared with the oil of impurity..."
O Lord, when indeed shall I stand before you with the lamp of knowledge? || 113 ||
O Lord, at what time—on which occasion—shall I be present before you, becoming intent solely on your worship, which consists in resting in non-difference from you? By what means?
By the lamp of knowledge—that is, by the very light of the awakening to reality—and not by external flowers and the like. As it has been said:
In the Śrīvijñānabhairava (page 120), it is said:
"What is called worship is not that firm mental state which is performed with flowers and other such offerings."
In the non-conceptual great void, that worship is indeed absorption through devotion.

Thus [it is said]. By what kind of lamp of knowledge? "Mala" is non-apprehension (akhyāti); because that very thing provides oiliness (*snigdhatā*) to the wicks of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is like oil. Those latent impressions—which are the diverse formative tendencies (*saṃskāra*) such as merit and demerit—are themselves the coils, because they constitute the winding. Being smeared (*akta*) or sprinkled by that [oil] means being moistened by it. These very [impressions], being the wicks due to their state of existing as the present, [are so described].
Because they are being raised up, he who necessarily burns them is the one [who sets them in motion]. || 113 ||
And the fulfillment of this prayer of yours, O Blessed One, is merely a matter of sport; thus he says:
"If you were to grant even a single moment [of grace] to one whose faults have been exhausted..."
O Śambhu, why will you not then bestow that state within the mind? || 114 ||

O Śambhu, if, by Your will alone, in the mind of those like me who are worthy of grace— whose defects have been exhausted and whose former bad impressions have ceased— there should be even for a single moment a foothold...
If you will establish yourself as the bestower of grace, then what will you not accomplish?
You fulfill every prayer at that very moment. As it has been said in the venerable *Mṛtyujidbhaṭṭāraka*:
If that reality is perceived for even the duration of a single blink of an eye,
from that moment on one is liberated and shall not undergo rebirth again.
Thus [ends the verse]. 114.
And therefore,
one should cultivate the thought: "I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, I am great."
O Lord, he who has you as his object of focus would possess an objective support (sālambanā). // 115 //
I alone am fortunate (*dhanya*), being enriched by "wealth" (*dhana*) in the form of the knowledge of non-difference from You;
likewise, I alone am one by whom the "task" (*kṛtya*)—characterized by the attainment of the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—has been "accomplished" (*kṛta*). Furthermore...

(122) "The Great One"— the realization or conviction that "I alone am the one who transcends all, and not one who remains as a limited lord (*bhedeśvara*")— becomes "with an objective support" (*sālambanā*), that is, grounded in reality, for anyone who [possesses it]. He who...
"Having you as his object of focus" (tvadālambanaḥ) means one for whom you, Maheśvara yourself, are the object of focus and refuge. || 115 ||
He demonstrates the superiority of devotion even over the Supreme Lord:
"Though you yourself are the creator of all that is auspicious and inauspicious,"
But devotion to you, O Lord, is the mother of auspiciousness alone. 116.

He is the Lord, the independent one; not only are Brahmā and the others, impelled by You, the agents of their own appropriate auspicious and inauspicious deeds, but even You Yourself are the agent—the progenitor—of all that is auspicious and inauspicious, namely the world consisting of *vidyā* and *māyā*. Yet, devotion to You...

Since the supreme birth of auspiciousness—which consists in the manifestation of non-difference from you—occurs [only] within one's own self when it is joined with devotion to you, there is great esteem for that self. || 116 ||

Now, it is the independent descent of power (*śaktipāta*) alone that brings about people who possess devotion consisting of absorption into their own self, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss; it does not, however—

"This [awakening] is caused by the equilibrium of karma, the ripening of impurity (mala), and so forth; nor is there a gradual ripening of impurity due to the presiding influence of the power of existence (bhava). This he stated in two verses beginning with "When the mind is serene, O Lord..."—the Master.
"Are you entering? Or rather, will this [city] become gracious because of your entry?"—thus the people waver in doubt. (117)
Furthermore, O Lord, this certainty here is indeed your own presiding presence, for it is a grace of the mind.
That is perfection; that is the supreme state. || 118 ||
(The Couple:
O Lord, when the mind—that is, consciousness—is serene, meaning its impurities have been fully ripened away.
(Page 124)

Or, when the equilibrium of karma has been established, people waver, wondering: "Do you enter [the body] yourself and exercise your power, or does it attain that grace—such as the ripening of impurities and so forth—through your entry, that is, through the exercise of your power? Thus the person is in doubt.

He doubts. Here, however, this is the certainty: that which is your presiding presence—the mere blossoming of your own sovereign power through the immersion of the concealment of one's own nature—is solely the grace of the mind, that is, of consciousness;
it is not at all something such as the ripening of impurities or the equilibrium of karma. For instance:

If the ripening of impurity (*malaparipāka*) or the equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*) is the cause of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), then what is the cause of that? If you say it is caused by the Lord’s empowering power (*bhagavacchakti*), then enough with that;
the Lord’s power itself will simply be the independent bestower of grace. If you say it is causeless, then [it would apply] to everyone.

If it is asked, "Why do they not arise simultaneously? Why do they arise at some particular time?"—[we reply that] since the beginningless limit of bondage (*bandhakoṭi*) for all [beings] is without start, why has no restriction of time been established? What can we do?
If it is argued that "it happens to someone, at some time, in some way," [we reply that this is due to] the fact that impurity (*mala*) acts as an obstructer by its own power.

(125) It is not possible for that which is stable and insentient to produce an effect characterized by maturation that is distinct [from its prior state] without the entry of a heterogeneous cause. Only a specific time [is required] in this regard.

If it is argued that [the soul] is an auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*), the question "What is this? receives no answer. If it is argued that the evolving impurity (*pariṇamanmala*) attains a particular state consisting of maturation (*paripākātmaka*), even here, as in the case of the transformation of milk into curd, there would be no entry of a contrary cause such as the sensation of heat.

The transformation of distinct characteristics is untenable. Just as in the view of those who maintain that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is independent [of karma], the diversity of the experience of karma and liberation occur according to the regulation of time; and just as in a universe whose sole agent is the Lord, the relationship of cause and effect among *māyā*, *kāla*, and so forth occurs sequentially, so too shall this come to pass.

And thus the logic of the "thunderbolt of fifty" (aśapañcāśanyāya) is arrived at; for according to that view, just as the Lord himself, through his sovereignty, appears as the various principles (tattvas) while manifesting an appearance of contraction,
so too does he appear in the form of the manifestation of the causal relation characterized by a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority inherent therein.

Even though it consists of the manifestation of succession through the diversity of determined actions and their fruits, there is no inherent reality whatsoever here belonging to time, action, or anything else.
(Page 126)

Just as that [Lord] manifests such a variety of enjoyments, so too, by His own sovereignty, does He manifest a variety of graces; thus, since there is no other entity here who undergoes either punishment or grace, this position is indeed faultless.

However, the position that [the result arises] from the ripening of impurities and so forth is indeed flawed by the aforementioned objections; thus, how could it be possible to accept it merely on the basis of an equality of probability? Furthermore, how could two contradictory actions of equal strength produce their results simultaneously, given both their contradiction and their equal strength?

If, due to the obstruction of those two [karmas], they are incapable of yielding their fruit, how could there ever be a descent of power (*śaktipāta*)? Or, why would another karma not yield its fruit at that same moment? If it is argued that "the time of ripening for that [other karma] is distinct because it was acquired at a different time," then how can there be a single time for those two [karmas] as well, which were both acquired at different times?

[Regarding] maturation: if it is argued that this occurs through the will of Īśvara, then let that very Blessed Lady, who is independent and bestows grace, be the cause; enough with this web of nonsense concerning the maturation of impurities and so forth. I have already examined this at length in my *Śrīsvacchandavivṛti* at the end of the fifth chapter, on the occasion of establishing the validity of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Just as the nature of impurity (*mala*) is described in the scriptures, and how its cessation occurs, that too has been fully established therein; therefore, there is no need for further elaboration here. Having internalized this very point, the author of the hymn [proceeds as follows].

It has been said: "The certainty here, moreover, is this: it is solely through your empowerment that there is the clarity of the mind—that is, of consciousness—and not even the ripening of impurities; and accomplishment is indeed your empowerment alone, for that is the supreme state. This is the essential truth here: that the Blessed One is nothing other than the power of consciousness itself.

Having assumed contraction through its own sovereignty, it manifests the manifold branches of the ground of consciousness—which is the nature of the transmigrating self—and then, by its own will alone, having pacified that contraction in certain instances, it vibrates in fullness; such is that supreme state. As it has been said by a certain great lord of yogis:
Indeed, this entire universe is filled with consciousness;
when the mind perpetually sets within the conscious Self, it remains perfectly established as non-different from that Consciousness.
The supreme samādhi is described as that in which the instruments [of perception] have been cast aside.
Thus [ends the section]. 118.

Having thus praised the true nature of the Blessed One through various elegant modes of expression, he speaks while expressing the aspiration: "May this state of being absorbed in the Blessed One remain unshakable in all circumstances."
O Lord, by your grace, may my speech, mind, activity, and body become [one with you].
The sole ornament of the existence of all beings. || 119 ||
If my speech in your praise has become permeated with meditation upon you,
may it remain so forever; and since that [speech] accompanies the mind, and the mind resides in the body, by way of those two,
let whatever there may be of those three— body, mind, and speech— be likewise [dedicated to you].

O Lord, O Master, who is a mass of consciousness and bliss— by Your grace, that is, by the removal of the concealment of Your own nature and the attainment of purity, may there always be Your very being within me, along with all effects such as the consideration, expression, and mental activity regarding objects.
It should be such that its sole ornament is the state of being identical with you. || 119 ||
In order to inspire those possessed of devotion to engage in seeking refuge and so forth, [the Lord] first uttered His own name, which is renowned for its power.
(Page 129)
By way of a concluding summary, he demonstrates the excellence of this hymn:
"The *Stavacintāmaṇi*, which bestows the fruits of manifold heart's desires."
Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa composed [this work], which is the abode of the fortune of devotion to Śambhu. || 120 ||
The Bhaṭṭa named Nārāyaṇa, whose power was renowned for his status as a great devotee of Maheśvara,

composed a hymn— a prayer that is itself a wish-fulfilling gem— to Śambhu, the Blessed Mahādeva, who bestows grace consisting of the recognition of one's own self as the mass of consciousness and bliss; of what nature is it?
To Him who bestows that great fruit— the fruit of manifold desires characterized by immersion into the Blessed One— for devotion alone,
being of the nature of identity with Maheśvara, is Lakṣmī, the supreme prosperity, and He is her eternal abode.

May the supreme splendor of immersion (samāveśa) always embrace those devoted to this [deity] through the hearing, recitation, and other practices of this hymn regarding the dwelling-place [of the Lord]. May there be auspiciousness! 120.
Born from Guṇāditya, he was preeminent among the multitude of virtues; filled with joy by the qualities of Śiva, he remained free from attachment to the world from his very childhood.
